**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr) on Surah 57, verse 1:**

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The opening of the surah with the mention of God's glorification (*tasbīh*) and His transcendence (*tanzīh*) indicates that the most important thing the surah contains is the affirmation of God's attributes with sublime qualities, which entail that He is exalted above what those who went astray have gone astray in ascribing to Him, namely describing Him with what does not befit His majesty. The first form of transcendence is the negation of any partner to Him in divinity, for oneness (*waḥdāniyya*) is the greatest attribute about whose essence the polytheists, the Manichaeans and their like from among the dualists, the adherents of the Trinity, and the Brahmins went astray. It is the attribute indicated by His proper name, *Allāh* (the proper noun), I mean the name ﴿Allāh﴾, as you know from the explanation of al-Fātiḥa (the Opening surah), that its origin is *al-Ilāh* (the God), i.e., the one who is singular in divinity.

He followed this name with lordly attributes that indicate God's perfection and His transcendence above deficiency, as will be explained. Thus this opening was a masterful introduction (*barāʿat istihlāl*) to this surah. For this reason, He followed His proper name with ten attributes that encompass the attributes of perfection, and they are: the Mighty, the Wise; to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; He gives life and causes death; and He is over all things capable; He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward; and He is, of all things, Knowing.

The verb of glorification is expressed in the past tense (*ṣīgha al-māḍī*, the perfect form) to indicate that His transcendence is an established matter, which God commanded His servants with previously, inspired into people, and deposited its indications in the states of things that have no choice, as indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows at dawn and dusk﴾ (al-Raʿd: 15), and His saying: ﴿There is nothing that does not glorify Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ (al-Isrāʾ: 44).

So in His saying "sabbaḥa" (glorified; the Arabic word *sabbaḥa* is kept as is) there is an allusion to the polytheists who neglected the most important glorification, which is glorifying Him above having a partner or rival.

The *lām* in His saying "li-Llāh" (*li-Llāh*, "to God") is the *lām* of specification (*lām al-tabyīn*). Its benefit is to add clarity to the connection of the object (*maʿmūl*) with its governing verb, because the verb of glorification is transitive by itself and does not need to be made transitive by a particle. God said: ﴿So prostrate to Him and glorify Him﴾ (al-Insān: 26), so the *lām* here is the counterpart of the *lām* in the expressions "I thanked you" (*shakartu laka*), "I advised you" (*naṣaḥtu laka*), and His saying, may He be exalted, "and we sanctify You" (*wa-nuqaddisu laka*), and their expressions *saqyan laka* and *raʿyan laka* (may you be watered, may you be pastured), whose original form is *saqyuka* and *raʿyuka*.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ encompasses all existing things, for *mā* (what) is a relative pronoun that includes rational beings and others, or it is specific to non-rational beings, and so it is used here by way of predominance (*taghlīb*, giving precedence to one category over another). All of them indicate God's transcendence above having a partner. Among them is indication by speech, such as the glorification of the prophets and believers; among them is indication by action, such as the glorification of the angels; and among them is indication by the testimony of the state, as the states of existing things reveal, in their need of the Maker who is singular in governance. If the generality of ﴿whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is restricted to those who are able to utter glorification, namely the rational beings, then the application of "glorification" to their glorification is literal.

And if the generality is taken in its apparent sense, it is necessary to interpret the verb "sabbaḥa" in a way that covers both the literal and the figurative, so that it is used in both its literal and figurative meanings together.

"The Mighty" (*al-ʿAzīz*) is the one who cannot be overcome, and this attribute negates the existence of a partner in divinity.

"The Wise" (*al-Ḥakīm*) is the one characterized by wisdom (*ḥikma*), which is placing actions where they are fitting. It is also knowledge that does not err, does not deviate, and nothing prevents its connection to the known things. Both were discussed in Surat al-Baqara. This attribute establishes that God's actions proceed according to preparing created things for what achieves the purpose for which they were created, and for this reason God strengthened them by guiding them through the mediation of the laws (*sharāʾiʿ*).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 2:**

﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things competent.﴾ This is an initial resumptive sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a sentence beginning a new topic), mentioning a great attribute of God whose object is the conditions of the beings in the heavens and the earth, especially those among them that have perception.

The meaning of this sentence implies the reason for glorifying God, Exalted is He, because the One to whom belongs the dominion of the higher worlds and the lower world deserves that people know the attributes of His perfection.

The definiteness of the predicate (*musnad*) indicates the restriction (*qasr*) of the predicate to the subject (*musnad ilayh*). This is a figurative restriction (*qasr idda'i*), because the dominion of others on earth is not taken into account, since it is a deficient dominion: kings are in need of someone to repel hostile attacks for them through alliances and armies, of someone to organize the system of the kingdom for them through viziers and commanders, and of collecting taxes and tribute and the like. Or it is a real restriction (*qasr haqiqi*), if the attribution of "dominion" is considered to be to the totality of "the heavens and the earth," for then no one has dominion over the whole earth, let alone the heavens together with it.

This is the meaning of His attribute, Exalted is He, "the King" (*al-Malik*), which was discussed at the end of Surat Al 'Imran.

The clause ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is an inclusive apposition (*badal ishtimal*) of the content of ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. This is because giving life and causing death are among the conditions of what is upon them, and the meaning of dominion over the heavens and the earth includes them.

The specification of these two actions by mention is for the sake of emphasis on them, because they indicate the subtle wisdom in the disposal of the heaven and the earth, and because it is evident that these two actions cannot be claimed by any created being to have any effect in them. It also serves as a reminder of the evidence for the place of resurrection, which the polytheists denied, and as an allusion to refuting their claim that their idols are divine, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿They have no power over death or life or resurrection﴾ [al-Furqan: 3]. From these two actions comes His description, Exalted is He, with the attribute "the Giver of life and the Causer of death."

The mention of giving life and causing death was already mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You were dead and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿and He is over all things competent﴾ serves the function of a concluding generalization (*tadhyil*, a summarizing final clause) for the clause ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾, to generalize what His saying ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ indicated as an explanation of the clause ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ It was joined by the conjunction "wa" (and), although the rule for a concluding generalization is that it should be disconnected (*maf'ul*), for the purpose of preferring to report about God, Exalted is He, the generality of power over every existing thing. This does not indicate the intent of a concluding generalization, because a concluding generalization is achieved by meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 3:

﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward﴾.

This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) in the context of clarifying that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. His dominion is everlasting across all times, and His disposal over them is in every state, for He is the First, the Eternal (al-Azali), and His existence is continuous both before the existence of every originated thing and after its annihilation, since Allah is the Abiding after the annihilation of whatever is in the heavens and the earth. This becomes apparent from the indication of effects upon the Effector, for the signs of His disposal are manifest to the one who reflects with reason, and this is the meaning of "al-Zahir" (the Outward), as will come. And the modes of His disposal are veiled from the senses, and this is the meaning of "al-Batin" (the Inward), exalted is He, as will come.

The pronoun "Huwa" is not a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), but a pronoun referring to the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah), given that we consider the sentence to be resumptive. Had you made it a pronoun of separation, the attributes "the First and the Last and the Outward and the Inward" would be predicates concerning the pronoun in "﴿He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾" [al-Hadid: 1].

Page 360

This sentence includes four predicates which are attributes of Allah, exalted is He.

As for the attribute "al-Awwal" (the First), its basic meaning is that which occurs before others in a state that is clarified by the attribution of this attribute to what indicates the state, of time or place. It may occur with an attribute. "Awwal" is a word indicating the state in which precedence occurred, and that state may be inferred from the context of speech. The attribute "al-Awwal" is not made clear except by what is connected to it of speech, and it is only conceived in relation to another described thing that is later than the one described as "awwal" in some state.

So the words of Imru' al-Qais:

"And Muhalhil of the poets, that is the first"

indicate that Muhalhil preceded other poets in poetry. His saying, exalted is He, "Say: I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit" [al-An'am: 14], means first of them in following Islam. His saying "And do not be the first to disbelieve in it" [al-Baqarah: 41] means first of them in disbelief. His saying "And the first of them said to the last of them" [al-A'raf: 39] means the first of them in entering the Fire.

The most well-known meaning of priority (al-awwaliyyah) is precedence in existence, that is, against non-existence. Do you not see that all the states in which one precedes another are existences of modes? So the description of Allah as "al-Awwal" means that His existence precedes every existent that has existed or will exist, without specifying a genus, species, or kind. Yet it is a relational attribute, not an essential one.

For this reason, no object of this attribute has been mentioned (with a kasra on the lam), nor anything indicating an object, because the intended meaning is that He is "the First" without restriction.

In the terminology of the theologians, this attribute is synonymous with the attribute of "qidam" (eternity without beginning).

Know that this attribute entails the attribute of absolute self-sufficiency (al-ghina al-mutlaq), which is the absence of need for a specifier, that is, a specifier that particularizes its existence instead of non-existence, because "al-Awwal" here means the existent by His essence without preceding non-existence; and the absence of need for a locus in which it subsists, like the subsistence of an accident in a substance.

Page 361

This entails that He, exalted is He, is singular in the attribute of existence, for if other than Allah had a necessary existence, Allah would not be described as "first". The existents other than Allah are contingent, and the contingent is not characterized by absolute priority; therefore oneness (al-wahdaniyyah) is established for Him. Then this priority in existence necessitates that all attributes of perfection be established for Allah by rational necessity, through clear implication in the more general sense (that which follows from conceiving its necessitating thing, and conceiving it entails a firm judgment of the correlation between them).

As for the attribute "al-Akhir" (the Last), it is the opposite of the First. Its basic meaning is: he who is preceded by a described thing with an attribute spoken of in the speech or referred to in it by what is mentioned of a relation to it, or its specification, in the manner previously stated concerning His saying "He is the First", like His saying, exalted is He, "until when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say to the first of them" [al-A'raf: 38], meaning the last of them in overtaking in the Fire; and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "The last of the people of Paradise to enter Paradise..." etc.; and the saying of al-Hariri in the second maqama, "and he sat among the last of the people", meaning the later groups in sitting. It is a relational attribute.

The description of Allah, exalted is He, as "al-Akhir" after describing Him as "al-Awwal", though the two attributes are opposites, requires the separation of the aspect of firstness and lastness. Since it has been established that His being "al-Awwal" is related to the existence of existents, it follows that His description as "al-Akhir" relates to the cessation of that existence, that is, He is "the Last" after all existents in the heavens and the earth. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, "He inherits the earth and whoever is upon it" [Maryam: 40], and His saying "Everything is perishing except His Face" [al-Qasas: 88].

So the meaning is estimated: "and the Last" in that, that is, in the continuance of existence which was established by His description as "the First". There is no indication in this that He is transient, subject to non-existence, since the attribute "al-Akhir" does not indicate cessation either by correspondence or by implication. This is the attribute of permanence (al-baqa') in the terminology of the theologians. Thus the meaning of "al-Akhir" returns to the meaning of "al-Baqi" (the Abiding). The attribute "al-Akhir" was chosen for mention because it is the requirement of eloquence, so that the antithesis (al-tibaq) between the two opposite attributes is complete. It is known among the theologians that permanence is not specific to Allah, exalted is He, and that it does not contradict origination, though there is disagreement about specifying which originated things are abiding. Unlike the attribute of eternity (qidam), which is specific to Allah, exalted is He, and contradicts origination.

Know that in His saying "He is the First and the Last" there is an indication of restriction (qasr) by way of defining both parts of the sentence.

Page 362

As for the restriction of priority to Allah, exalted is He, in the attribute of existence, it is evident. As for the restriction of lastness to Him in that, which is the meaning of permanence: if by it is meant permanence in the worldly realm, the problem of contradiction arises with what has been reported of the permanence of souls, and the hadith that "the coccyx bone does not perish, and from it the human being is restored." The resolution of this problem is that the restriction be taken as rhetorical (idda'i), to disregard the permanence of anything other than Him, since it is permanence not necessary in itself, rather it is by the making of Allah, exalted is He.

The combination between the two attributes "﴿the First and the Last﴾" contains the embellishment of antithesis (tibaq).

The more preponderant view is that "al-Zahir" is derived from manifestation (al-zuhur), which is the opposite of concealment. His description, exalted is He, with it is then a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), for the attribution of manifestation in reality is the manifestation of the proofs of His essential attributes to the people of reflection, inference, and contemplation of the signs of the world. Thus the attribute comprises His essential attribute, which is existence, since the proofs of His existence are clear and evident, and His other attributes evidenced by His act of power, knowledge, life, and will; and the attributes of action, of creation, provision, giving life and causing death, as you know from His saying "He is the First", and the attributes indicating His transcendence above deficiency, or what they indicate of His exaltation above deficiency, such as the attribute of oneness, eternity, permanence, absolute self-sufficiency, and dissimilarity to originated things. This meaning is the one suited by its contrast with "al-Batin".

It is also permissible that it be derived from manifestation in the sense of dominance, as in His saying, exalted is He, "for if they gain the upper hand over you they will stone you" [al-Kahf: 20]. So the meaning of describing Him, exalted is He, as "al-Zahir" is that He is the Dominant.

This does not suit its contrast with "al-Batin" except on the consideration of the embellishment of ambiguity (husn al-iham). What occurred in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in Sahih Muslim from the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "You are the Zahir, so there is nothing above You" — the meaning of the fa' of consequence (fa' al-tafri') in it is that His manifestation, exalted is He, is the cause of the negation that anything be above Allah in manifestation, that is, in the indication of the proofs of His existence and His being described by the attributes of perfection. So the fa' indicates consequence, not explanation.

And "al-Batin" the hidden: it is said "batana", if it was hidden, and its verbal noun is butun.

The meaning of describing Him, exalted is He, as "al-Batin" is the description of His essence and quiddity, since He is veiled from the perception of the outward senses. He, exalted is He, said: "Vision does not perceive Him" [al-An'am: 103].

Page 363

The restriction in His saying "﴿and the Outward and the Inward﴾" is a rhetorical restriction, because the manifestation of Allah, exalted is He, in both senses is a manifestation which nothing else approaches, and His inwardness, exalted is He, is not like the inwardness of hidden things, since no one has any hope of perceiving His essence or knowing the details of His dispositions.

The combination of describing Him as "al-Zahir" in the preponderant sense and "al-Batin" is like the combination of describing Him as "﴿al-Awwal wa al-Akhir﴾", as you have just known. In the combining of them is the embellishment of correspondence (tibaq).

The benefit of applying the two opposite attributes to the Name of Allah here is to draw attention to the greatness of the station of Allah, exalted is He, so that the learned may reflect on their placements. Know that the three waws (conjunctions) occurring between these four attributes have a single meaning, each one requiring the conjunction of an attribute.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The first waw means that He combines the two attributes of firstness and lastness; the third means that He combines outwardness and inwardness; and the middle one means that He combines the two first attributes and the two latter attributes. End of quote. This is a far-fetched reading for which there is no need nor evidence. Had that been intended, he would have said: "He is the First, the Last, and the Outward, the Inward," with two waws dropped. The meaning al-Zamakhshari sought is required by the meanings of these attributes without any difference in the meanings of the waws.

﴿And He is, of everything, Knowing﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿He is the First and the Last﴾, etc.; the attribute of His knowledge is conjoined to the attribute of His essence. A parallel to this sentence occurred at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 4:

﴿He it is Who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾.

The position of this sentence is that of a resumptive new statement (isti'naf), like the position of the sentence ﴿He is the First and the Last﴾ [al-Hadid: 3], so this is a second resumptive statement, which serves as evidence for God the Exalted's sole divinity, so that they may desist from associating others with Him.

It also serves as an elaboration of the content of the sentence ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 2] and the sentence ﴿and He is Able over all things﴾ [al-Hadid: 2], for the One Who created the heavens and the earth is capable of magnificent origination.

The establishment upon the Throne is a figurative expression (tamthil) for the dominion mentioned in His saying ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 2].

This is the meaning of His name "the Creator" (al-Khaliq), and something close to this verse has preceded at the beginning of Surah al-A'raf.

* * *

﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it, and what descends from the heaven and what ascends into it﴾.
This is a resumptive statement to establish the all-encompassing nature of God the Exalted's knowledge of everything. Thus it serves as an explanation of the sentence ﴿and He is Able over all things﴾ [al-Hadid: 2] and the sentence ﴿and He is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Hadid: 3], proceeding according to the method of al-nashr (unfolding) following al-laff (folding), in order. The parallel of this verse has preceded in Surah Saba', so refer to that.

﴿And He is with you wherever you are, and God is Seeing of what you do﴾. It is the conjunction (atf) of a specific meaning upon a general meaning that includes it and other things, for the purpose of emphasizing the conjoined element.
Being "with" (al-ma'iyyah) is a metonymic figurative expression (tamthil kinai) for knowledge of all His states.

And "ayna ma" (wherever) is a compound adverb formed from (ayna), which is a noun of place, and (ma), the redundant particle that serves to indicate the generalization of places.

The sentence ﴿God is Seeing of what you do﴾ is a complement to the content of ﴿He is with you wherever you are﴾, and its proper form was that it should not be conjoined, but it was conjoined to give preference to the aspect of the information it contains concerning this attribute.

﴿His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. This repeats its counterpart at the beginning of this surah, and it is repeated so that the statement ﴿And to Allah are returned all matters﴾ may be built upon it. The mention at the beginning of the surah was built upon [the fact of] His disposal of existent things, which are capable of life and death in this world, while the mention here is built upon the fact that the affairs of all existent things return to His disposal.

Placing the predicate first serves to restrict divinity to Him, may He be exalted, which conveys the attribute of Oneness.

﴿And to Allah are returned all matters﴾ is conjoined to ﴿His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ as a conjunction of the particular in one respect to the general within it, concerning the matters that occur in this world, and as a conjunction of something different concerning the matters that take place on the Day of Resurrection, as will become clear in the explanation of the meaning of "al-umur" (matters).

*Al-umur* is the plural of *amr*. It is well known in the language that *amr* is a term for a matter or an occurrence, so it encompasses both actions and statements.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Here *al-umur* means all existent things, because *al-amr*, *al-shay'* (thing) and *al-mawjud* (existent) are terms commonly applied to all existents, both their accidents and their substances." End of quotation. I have not seen this from anyone else. In *al-Mahsul* (a work of usul al-fiqh) and its commentary, and in those who followed it among the books of usul al-fiqh, it is stated that the word *amr* is homonymous (*mushtarak*) among the meanings of act, statement, affair and thing. I have not found this ascribed to any recognised authority, nor have they brought an example for it that is free from scrutiny, and I do not think this is from the language.

If we adopt the well-known usage in the language, the meaning is: the actions of people return to Allah, that is, they return at the Gathering (al-hashr), and what is intended is the return of their people for recompense for their deeds, since return does not apply to the realities themselves. Thus the conjunction of ﴿And to Allah are returned all matters﴾ completes the sentence ﴿His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: His is the dominion of the worlds in this life, and He has disposal over the deeds of the rational beings among its people in the Hereafter.

If we adopt the inclusion of the term *al-umur* to essences, it conveys the affirmation of resurrection, that is:

[Page 366]

the essences which existed in this world will come to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense them for their deeds.

On both interpretations, its import is the same as the import of His name *al-Muhaymin* (the Guardian).

The definite plural form in *al-umur* is one of the forms of generality.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before what it relates to serves emphasis (*li'l-ihtimam*), not restriction (*li'l-qasr*). There is no basis for a real restriction, nor any reason for a restriction relative to others (*qasr idafi*), since there is no one among the disbelievers who denies resurrection, nor anyone who claimed that people come under the disposal of other than Allah.

*Al-ruju'* (return) is used metaphorically for being in a place other than the one one was in, without a prior departure from that place.

The explicit mention of the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalalah*), rather than saying "and to Him are returned all matters," is so that the sentence stands independently with what it indicates, and so it becomes like a proverb, fit to be circulated.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read *turja'u* (with the first letter *ta'* pronounced with a *damma*, and the *jim* with a *fatha*), meaning that someone causes it to return, namely Allah, by compulsion. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, Ya'qub, and Khalaf read *tarji'u* (with the *ta'* with a *fatha* and the *jim* with a *kasra*), meaning: they return of their own accord, because they are subjected to that by their appointed terms.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 6:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night.﴾

The occasion of mentioning this sentence is that the determination of night and day and their succession are among the divine acts witnessed in the affairs of the heavens and the earth and in the circumstances that surround human affairs. Thus this sentence is a badal al-ishtimal (a comprehensive substitute clause) for the sentence ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 5].

It also fits the content of the sentence ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Hadid: 5] as a reminder to the polytheists that the one who disposes of the cause of perishing is Allah, the Exalted. For they believed that night and day are what destroy people. Al-A'sha said:

"Did you not see Iram and 'Ad? Night and day destroyed them both."

﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend of that in which He has made you successors. So those among you who have believed and spent will have a great reward.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) which occupies the position of a conclusion after the argument. The beginning of the surah established the subjection of all creatures to Allah the Exalted, and that He, the Exalted, is the one who disposes of them by bringing into being and annihilating and otherwise; so He is capable over them. And that He is All-Knowing of their conditions, aware of what their hearts conceal, and that they will return to Him, so He will call them to account. Therefore the situation was ready for conveying to them the reminder to believe in Him, a belief not mixed with association (shirk), and to believe in His Messenger ﷺ, since his truthfulness had become clear through the past proofs which indicated the soundness of what he had informed them of, which had been the object of their doubt and denial, as His saying indicates: ﴿And the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord﴾ [al-Hadid: 8].

This is the reason for the conjunction of "wa rasulihi" (and His Messenger) with the object of belief, although the preceding verses mentioned only the evidences of the attributes of Allah and not the Messenger ﷺ.

The address with "Amanu" (believe) is to the polytheists, and the verse is Meccan according to what is narrated concerning the conversion of 'Umar. This is the reading that fits the connection of His saying ﴿And why do you not believe in Allah?﴾ [al-Hadid: 8] etc. with it.

The spending commanded is the spending that belief calls to after belief has been attained, which is spending upon the poor. The specific mention of spending is an honouring of its status. The people of Jahiliyyah spent only on pleasures, boasting, gambling, and drinking wine, and the Qur'an described them with this in many places, such as His saying ﴿Indeed, he did not believe in the Mighty Allah, and did not urge the feeding of the needy﴾ [al-Haqqah: 33], and His saying ﴿Nay, you do not honour the orphan﴾ [al-Fajr: 17], ﴿nor do you urge one another to feed the needy﴾ [al-Fajr: 18], ﴿and you devour inheritance, devouring greedily﴾ [al-Fajr: 19], ﴿and you love wealth with abundant love﴾ [al-Fajr: 20], and His saying ﴿Rivalry in worldly increase diverts you until you visit the graves﴾ [al-Takathur: 1], to the end of the surah.

It has been said: it was revealed concerning the expedition of Tabuk, meaning the spending for equipping the army of hardship (jaysh al-'usrah). Ibn 'Atiyyah said, quoting al-Dahhak. In that case the verse is Madinan, and His saying "Amanu" (believe) is a command to persist in belief, like His saying ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [an-Nisa': 136].

It is also possible that it is a command addressed to those in whose souls there remained some hypocrisy or doubt, and who had withheld their hands from equipping the army of hardship, as the Exalted said ﴿The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [at-Tawbah: 67] up to His saying ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾ [at-Tawbah: 67]. So when they heard the address, they knew that they were the ones intended, in the manner of what is in the verses of Surah Bara'ah. But it appears that by the year of the expedition of Tabuk, there remained among the hypocrites no number worth considering, so an address like this would not be directed to them.

The relative pronoun is used in His saying ﴿of that in which He has made you successors﴾ rather than saying "and spend of your wealth, or of what Allah has provided you," because of what the relative clause contains of alerting to the heedlessness of the hearers regarding the fact that wealth belongs to Allah; He made people like successors (khala'if) concerning it, in its disposal for a period. So when He commanded them to spend from it upon His servants, it was incumbent upon them to comply, just as the treasurer complies with the command of the owner of the wealth when he orders him to dispatch some of it to whomever he designates.

The sin and ta' in "mustakhlafin" (made successors) are for intensifying the occurrence of the act, not for requesting (talab), since the request is derived from the verb "ja'alakum." It is also possible that they are for emphasising the request.

The fa' in His saying ﴿So those among you who have believed and spent will have a great reward﴾ is a consequential and causal particle upon the command to believe and spend, to indicate its causation, as if it were said: because those who believed and spent, We have prepared for them a great reward.

The meaning according to the reading that the verse is Meccan: that those among you who believed and spent, i.e., preceded you in belief and spending, for them is a great reward; i.e., seize it and make up what they have outstripped you in.

The "min" (among) is for partitiveness, i.e., those who believed, and they are part of your people.

It is also permissible that the two past-tense verbs in His saying ﴿So those among you who have believed and spent﴾ are used in the sense of the present tense, to alert to the realisation of that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 8:

﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not believe in Allah, while the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord, and He has taken your covenant, if you are [truly] believers?﴾

The apparent usage of expressions like His saying ﴿What is [wrong] with you that you do not believe?﴾ is that it is an interrogative used in the sense of reproach and wonder, and this is what fits the fact that the command in His saying ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 136] is used in the sense of a demand (talab), not of continuance (dawam).

The clause "you do not believe" (la tu'minun) may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in the stative verb (al-kawn) that the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) depends upon, as when you say: "What is with you standing?" meaning: "What are you doing while standing?" The implied meaning is: "And what is [the matter] with you being disbelievers in Allah," i.e., what has happened to you in the state of not believing?

The clause ﴿and the Messenger calls you﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, and the waw is the waw of circumstance, not of conjunction, so the two are interlocking circumstances (hal mutadakhilan). The meaning is: What prevents you from believing when the Messenger has made clear to you, from the verses of the Qur'an, that which contains sufficient communication and proof that belief in Allah is true? There is no excuse for you for not believing in Allah, for the evidences of its truth have come to you. It is therefore determined that your persistence in not believing is obstinacy and stubbornness.

On this reading, the covenant taken from them is a covenant from Allah, i.e., something similar to the covenant, namely the deposit of belief in the existence of Allah and His oneness in the human nature (fitrah). It is as if a covenant had been taken from every one of mankind in pre-eternity and at the condition of creation, so it is a natural law (namus fitri). This is an allusion to His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying]: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and it has preceded in Surat al-A'raf.

So the pronoun in "akhadha" refers to the name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah) in His saying ﴿Do you not believe in Allah﴾. The meaning is: if souls were free of obstinacy, of deception, and of misguidance, they would be inclined toward perceiving the existence of the Creator and His oneness. There has come to them from the call of the Messenger ﷺ what uncovers from them what the calls of the leaders of disbelief and misguidance had veiled from their perception.

The clause ﴿if you are believers﴾ is resumptive (musta'nifah), and the answer of the condition is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿and the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord, and He has taken your covenant﴾.

The active participle in His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ is used for the future, by the indication of its occurrence in the context of a condition, i.e., the cause that requires you to believe has already come about, both the apparent cause and the hidden cause fixed in the innate disposition (jibillah).

This meaning is supported by the fact that the apparent form of the command in His saying ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hadid: 7] is for seeking the bringing about of belief, as has preceded in its explanation, and that the verse is Meccan.

Al-Jumhur read "akhadha" in the active voice with "mithaqakum" in the accusative, the pronoun referring to the name of Majesty. Abu 'Amr read it "ukhidha" in the passive voice with "mithaqukum" in the nominative.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 9:

﴿He it is who sends down to His servant clear signs, that He may bring you out from darkness into light. Indeed, Allah is toward you Kind and Merciful.﴾

This is a third resumptive statement (isti'naf), by which the address turned to the believers. It appears that this verse is the beginning of the Medinan verses in this surah, and this becomes clearer through the conjunction of His words ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the cause of Allah﴾ [al-Hadid: 10] and what follows, as will come shortly.

Although the address here is suitable for confirming what the sentence ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah, while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord﴾ [al-Hadid: 8] conveyed, the style of the composition and what is conjoined to this sentence require that it be a transitional resumption, which is of the excellence of transition (husn al-takhallus) to addressing the Muslims. Nor is the indication of confirming what precedes lost, because the confirmation arises from the linking of the two meanings: the meaning of the previous sentence and the meaning of this following sentence.

So this sentence, by its placement, its meaning, its reason, and what is conjoined to it, conveys explanation (bayan), emphasis (ta'kid), causation (ta'lil), concluding summation (tadhyil), and transition (takhallus) to a new purpose. These are purposes that it gathered together in a manner that reached the level of inimitability in conciseness, while each sentence among them is independent with a great meaning of inference, reminder, guidance, and favor.

Al-Ra'uf: one of the forms of intensification in attachment to ra'fah (tenderness), which is the aversion to causing harm to another.

Al-Rahim: from mercy (rahmah), which is the love of bringing good to another.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "la-ra'ufun" (لَرَءُوفٌ) with a waw after the hamza, according to the well-known dialect. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read it without a waw after the hamza, and this is a dialect, and perhaps it is a lightening (takhfif). Jarir said:

It sees for the Muslims over it a right like the action of the father, the tender (ra'uf) and merciful (rahim).

The confirmation of the statement with "inna" (إنَّ) and the lam in His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is toward you Kind and Merciful (la-ra'ufun rahim)﴾ is because the polytheists, in their turning away from the call of Islam, had considered it an offense against them, their forefathers, and their gods. They said ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger? He would have almost led us away from our gods had we not been steadfast in them﴾ [al-Furqan: 41]. This indicates that His words, ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hadid: 7] up to here, are Meccan. If the verse is Medinan, then it is because the hypocrites were in that same state.

[Page 373]

﴿And why should you not spend in the way of Allah, when to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth?﴾ Spending in the way of Allah, in its well-known sense, which is spending on the equipment of jihad, did not occur except after the Hijrah, because "the way of Allah" (sabil Allah) in the Qur'an has come to be used predominantly for jihad. This is supported by His words that follow it: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the Conquest﴾, since the natural expectation is that this verse was revealed in connection with that. Had spending been understood in the sense of charity (sadaqat), it would imply that the verse is Medinan, because spending in this sense is applied only to charity given to the believers, and so the polytheists would not be blamed for failing to do it.

Accordingly, the address is directed to the believers, and the address has been repeated in a form different from the one with which it began.

Among its subtleties is that it is directed at the hypocrites (munafiqun), who outwardly appear to be Muslims but inwardly are polytheists; they are the ones who were stingy with spending.

The reason this verse, though Medinan, is joined to the Meccan part of the surah is the correspondence of covering the states of those who withhold spending, both from the disbelievers and from the believers, as an indirect warning against the traits of the people of disbelief, since before it He said: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7].

[Page 373 continued]
Ma (ما) is interrogative, used to express reproach and rebuke for their not spending in the way of Allah.

An (أنْ) is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), and the verbal noun formed from it together with the verb it governs (al-fi'l al-mansub biha) is in a position of genitive, either with the preposition li- (ل, "for") or with a deleted fi (في, "in"). The meaning is: "What has happened to you in your not spending?", that is, that which has occurred is a reprehensible matter.

It is reported from al-Akhfash that an is extra (za'idah), so it is like His words: ﴿And why do you not believe in Allah?﴾ [al-Hadid: 8]. That its governing of the following verb does not prevent it from being considered extra is because the extra particle may govern just as the extra preposition does, and this was previously discussed at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: "And why should we not fight in the way of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The waw (و) in ﴿and to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾ is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal), and the clause is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "tunfiqu" (you spend), in that the generality of "the heavens and the earth" encompasses what is in them, and so it encompasses the addressees. That generality is the connecting link. The sense is: "To Allah belongs the inheritance of what is in the heavens and the earth," and His inheritance includes you.

The meaning is: a denial of their not spending their wealth in that to which Allah has called them to spend, while they will perish and leave their wealth to whomever Allah has decreed its destination to be. So if they spent some of their wealth in what Allah commanded them, they would attain the pleasure of Allah and benefit from wealth that is destined to pass to those who will inherit from them.

The annexation of "inheritance" (miras) to "the heavens and the earth" is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object (idafat al-masdar ila al-maf'ul), and it involves an omitted noun, its estimated form being "its people" (ahliha). What is intended is not the inheritance of the essence of the heavens and the earth, because that occurs only after the extinction of people, and so it would not affect the aim of urging them to spend.

* * *

[Page 374]
﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the Conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought. And to each Allah has promised the best. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), arising from what occurs to the minds of many of the listeners: that they were late in spending, not intending to abandon it, but that they would make it up.

Incorporated into it is the preference of the jihad of some of the mujahidin over that of others, due to the fact that spending in the way of Allah includes the mujahid's spending on himself for equipment and provisions, and his spending on others who have not completed their equipment or provisions. Also, among the Muslims are those who are able to fight but not able to spend, so it was intended not to neglect mentioning them among the people of this virtue, since spending in it is a means to it.

The apparent meaning of the word "Conquest" (al-fath) is the conquest of Makkah, since this definite noun has become a proper designation (alam) by dominance for the conquest of Makkah. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

The reason those who spent and fought before the Conquest are greater in rank is that the period before the conquest of Makkah was a time of weakness for the Muslims, because the people of disbelief were the majority of the Arabs. When Makkah was conquered, the rest of Quraysh and the Arabs entered Islam. So spending and fighting before the Conquest were harder on the souls of the Muslims, due to their scarcity of resources and their small numbers facing the enemy's large force. Do you not see that they were required to stand firm before the enemy even when the enemy's number was ten times that of the Muslims in battle? He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿If there are among you twenty who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 65].

It has been said that what is meant by the Conquest is the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. This is the view of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, and of al-Zuhri, al-Sha'bi, and Amir ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and al-Tabari chose it. What supports what al-Tabari narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. This is the most fitting, given that this surah is partly Meccan and partly Medinan, which implies that its Medinan part is close in time to their period of residence in Makkah. The application of "Conquest" to the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah also occurs in His words: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest﴾ [al-Fath: 1].

[Page 375]
"Man anfaqa" (those who spent) is general, encompassing everyone who spent. It has been said that what is intended by it is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, because he spent all his wealth from the first appearance of Islam.

The negation of equality is intended as a negation of equality in virtue and reward. The negation of equality in an attribute implies the affirmation of the basic existence of that attribute for all of those of whom equality is negated. So the negation of equality is a metonymy (kinayah) for preferring one of the two sides and diminishing the other side by a varying degree.

The superior side and the inferior side are identified by context or by explicit statement in the speech. Placing one of the two sides first in mention after the negation of equality does not necessarily imply that it is the preferred one. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Not equal are those who sit [at home] among the believers, other than those with a disability, and those who strive in the way of Allah with their wealth and their lives﴾ [al-Nisa': 95], and this verse placed the preferred side first. The same applies to the saying of al-Samaw'al:

"So the knowing man and the ignorant man are not equal."

This implication is emphasized by His words: ﴿Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought﴾, meaning: those who spent after the Conquest and fought after the Conquest. The comparative form (ism al-tafdil) indicates participation in what the comparative is derived from, together with an excess for the one about whom the comparative is stated in the attribute from which it is derived. So both groups have a great rank.

The phrase "those who spent before the Conquest" has been omitted for brevity, since the verb of equality indicates it inevitably. The estimated form is: "Not equal are those who spent before the Conquest and those who spent after it."

"Rank" (darajah) is used metaphorically for virtue, because rank entails ascent, so the attribute of ascent is noticed in it. Then virtue and nobility are likened to ascent, and so it is expressed by "rank". Thus "rank" is among the generic nouns in which the attributes of descriptions are noticed, like the noun "lion" with the attribute of courage in the saying of the Kharijite:

"A lion against me, but in wars an ostrich."

His words ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ serve as a safeguard against someone who might suppose that the comparative form has lost its comparative sense through exaggeration, as in His words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, the prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me"﴾ [Yusuf: 33], meaning: "beloved to me rather than what they invite me to of disobedience."

He expressed it with "al-husna" (the best) to show that the rank is the rank of the best, so that the safeguard has a meaning beyond emphasis, which is the clarification it contains.

Al-husna (the best) is a Qur'anic and Islamic technical designation (laqab) that refers to the good things of the Hereafter. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26].

His words "minkum" (among you) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "man anfaqa"; its original position is an adjectival description, but it has been placed first for emphasis, to hasten this attribute.

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is used in His words ﴿Those are greater in rank﴾ instead of a pronoun, because of the honor and exaltation that the demonstrative indicates, and to draw attention to the fact that those referred to are deserving of what is stated after the demonstrative, on account of what was mentioned before it of the information given. A similar case is His words ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] after His words ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing, who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2–3], and so on.

The majority of readers recite ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ with the accusative "kullan" (each), as the first object placed before its verb according to the pattern of the construction with the omitted pronoun (al-ishtighal bi al-damir al-mahdhuf), for brevity. Ibn 'Amir recited it with the nominative (al-raf') as the subject (mubtada'). Both are two permissible readings in the ishtighal construction, equal in standing.

This verse is a foundational principle regarding the superiority of people of virtue in respect of what they have been preferred in, and that virtue is established for those who embraced Islam after the Conquest, from among the people of Makkah and others. How evil is what some historians say, in expressions that imply disparagement of those from Quraysh who embraced Islam after the Conquest, such as the term "the freed ones" (al-tulaqa')! Such things arise only from tribal or partisan grudges in the souls. Allah says: ﴿And do not defame one another, nor call each other by nicknames. How wretched is the name of defiance after faith. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

The clause ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyil), and the waw is parenthetical (waw i'tirad). The meaning is: Allah knows the causes of spending, its times, and its excuses, and He knows the states of jihad and the intentions of the mujahidin, so He gives each doer according to the intention of his action.

[p. 377]

﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him and he will have a generous reward?﴾ The position of this sentence is that of a causal explanation and clarification of the sentence ﴿And to each God has promised the best [reward]﴾ [al-Hadid: 10]. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD). The meaning is: the likeness of one who spends in the way of God is like the likeness of one who lends to God, and God's recompense for him is like the case of a borrower dealing with one who has treated his loan well and has been good in repaying it to him.

"Man" (مَن) is interrogative, as is its usual role when it is followed by a demonstrative or a relative pronoun, and "alladhi yuqridu" (who lends) is its predicate. "Dha" (ذا) is inserted to bring to mind the state of the borrower as though he were a present, near person.

From al-Farra' (ذا) is a ṣila, that is, an extra element used merely for emphasis, as many grammarians have said that (ذا) in (ماذا) is cancelled. Al-Farra' said: "I saw it in the codex of ʿAbd Allah [Ibn Masʿud] as 'manadha alladhi,' with the nūn joined to the dhāl." End of quotation.

The interrogative is used, figuratively, to mean exhortation (taḥrīḍ), because the one who urges another to an act customarily searches for someone to perform it and seeks to identify him in order to entrust it to him or to reward him for it.

The goodly loan (al-qard al-ḥasan) is the loan that has fully achieved the excellences of its kind: that it is given willingly and with a cheerful face toward the borrower, and is free of anything that implies obligation or that narrows the term of repayment. The thing compared here to the goodly loan is spending in the way of God, whose abandonment is forbidden in the words of God: ﴿And why should you not spend in the way of God?﴾ [al-Hadid: 10].

The majority read "fa-yuḍāʿifuhu" with an alif after the ḍād. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub read "fa-yuḍaʿʿifuhu," without an alif and with a shadda on the ʿayn.

The fa' in the clause "fa-yuḍāʿifuhu lahu" is the fa' of causation, because the multiplication is caused by the loan. The majority read the verb "yuḍāʿifu" in the nominative, considering it coordinated with "yuqridu."

The meaning is an exhortation to lending and the attainment of multiplication, because lending is the cause of multiplication, so the action of bringing about the loan is treated as though it were the action of bringing about the multiplication.

[p. 378]

Or it is considered that there is an elided subject, so that the clause is nominal in its underlying structure, and the verbal predicate then follows the subject, serving to strengthen the predicate and affirm its occurrence. And this clause is considered an answer to the relative "man," with the relative taking on the meaning of a conditional (ishrāb al-mawṣūl bi-maʿnā al-sharṭ), a widespread usage in the Qur'an.

Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Yaʿqub read it ("kullun ʿalā qirāʾatihi," each according to his own reading) in the accusative, as an answer to the interrogative.

The meaning of ﴿and he will have a generous reward﴾: he will have the most precious kind of rewards, because "karīm" in everything means precious and noble, as was mentioned earlier in the words of God: ﴿Indeed, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾ [al-Naml: 29], in the Surah of al-Naml. The generous reward is placed as the counterpart of the goodly loan, so that a qualified noun is matched with a qualifier of the same kind.

Multiplication (al-muḍāʿafa) means that the amount is equalled, so the meaning is that He gives him double the amount of his loan.

What is intended here is that He multiplies it many times over, as He said: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain that produces seven ears﴾ [al-Baqara: 261], the verse in Surah al-Baqara.

And He said: ﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over﴾ [al-Baqara: 245]. The pronoun of the object in "yuḍāʿifuhu" refers to the goodly loan, and the speech is according to an elision of a genitive, its estimated form being: "so that He multiplies its recompense for him." This is because the loan here is an image drawn from the state of the customary loan among people, so its multiplication is like the multiplication of the wealth of the lender, and that was before the prohibition of usury.

The reward (al-ajr) is what exceeds the repayment of the loan in the form of a gift that the borrower bestows upon the one who lent to him when he finds a means. It is about this that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The best of you are those who are best in repayment." And God said: ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [al-Nisa': 40].

The apparent meaning is that this reward is forgiveness, as in God's words: ﴿If you lend to God a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you, and God is Most Appreciative, Forbearing﴾ [al-Taghabun: 17], in the Surah of al-Taghabun. This includes spending in charities. God said: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who lend to God a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a generous reward﴾ [al-Hadid: 18].

[p. 379]

This is what the statement of the Prophet ﷺ explains: "Charity extinguishes sins as water extinguishes fire." That is, it is an increase over its multiplication, like all the good deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 12:

﴿On the Day you will see the believing men and the believing women, their light running before them and on their right hands: "Good news for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph."﴾

Since it is known that the multiplication of reward and the giving of the wage take place on the Day of Recompense, it is most likely that his saying "On the Day you see the believing men" is governed by an omitted verb, whose estimate is: "Mention" (udhkur), as an emphasis on what takes place on that Day of reward for the believing men and women, and of deprivation for the hypocritical men and women. For this reason "yawm" is repeated, so that each group is singled out with mention of what belongs to its condition on that Day.

On this basis, the sentence is connected to what precedes it by means of this governance. Moreover, within the structure of the speech it is also valid to make it an adverbial complement related to ﴿He will multiply it for him, and he will have a generous reward﴾ [al-Hadid: 11], by way of transition (takhallus) to mention what occurs on that Day of good for its people and of evil for its people.

On the first aspect, the sentence is a fresh, initiating resumption (istiʼnaf ibtida'i) for the occasion of mentioning the reward of those who spend, so it follows up by explaining some of the virtues of the believers. On the second aspect, it is connected to what precedes it by means of this governance.

The address in "tara" (you see) is to an unspecified person, so that it conforms to the pattern of the addresses before it; that is, "a Day on which the beholder sees," and the seeing is visual. "Yawm" is indeclinable on the fatha because it is annexed to a verbal sentence, though it may also be a case-ending fatha, since what is annexed to the present tense permits both possibilities.

The reason for coordinating "al-mu'minat" (the believing women) with "al-mu'minin" (the believing men) here, and in its like in Medinan Qur'an, is to draw attention to the fact that the portions of women in this religion are equal to the portions of men, except in those few rulings specific to them, which have their own specific evidences. This refutes what the Jews held concerning women, placing them in a state of cursed and deprived of most acts of obedience.

We have explained some of this when discussing His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the free for the free﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The light mentioned here is real light, which Allah places in their passage from the place of gathering, as an honour to them and an elevation of them on that gathering.

The meaning is: "their light runs while they run," so this is omitted, because light only runs when its owner runs; otherwise it would separate from him and leave him.

The annexing of "light" to their pronoun, and placing its location "before them and on their right hands," shows that it is a light belonging to their very selves, with which they were honoured.

Consider the meaning of this annexation to their pronoun, and the metaphor in His saying "yas'a" (runs), and the reason for specifying the light to the front direction and to the right hands; all of that is in Surat al-Tahrim.

The "ba'" in "wa bi-aymanihim" (and on their right hands) is in the sense of "'an" (on the side of), and he restricted mention to the right hands, honouring them, and this is by way of economy (iktifa'), that is, "and on their two sides."

It is also permissible for the "ba'" to be for accompaniment (mulabasa), and the light accompanying the right hand is the light of the book of good deeds, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for him who is given his book in his right hand, he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 7]. The book of good deeds is guidance, so the word "light" is used in both its literal and figurative senses, namely guidance and blessing.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "From this verse is derived the carrying of a candle by the one who is freed," end. Perhaps he is pointing to a custom familiar among them of placing in the hand of the slave whom they free a lit candle which he carries at the hour of his manumission; but I have not found this in the words of anyone else.

"Al-bushra" (the good news) is the verbal noun of "bashshara," and it is the informing of a report that gladdens the one informed. The verbal noun is used for the object, which is a common usage, like "al-khalq" meaning "the created thing." That is: that by which you are given good news: "gardens." The speech is with two elided annexed nouns, whose estimate is: "an announcement of entry into gardens," as His saying "abiding therein" indicates.

The clause "Good news for you" to its end is the object of an omitted saying, and the estimate is: "It is said to them," that is, it is said from the side of the Holy (al-Quds), which the angels say, or they hear a speech that Allah creates, which they know to be from the side of the Holy.

The clause "That is the great triumph" may be part of the speech reported by the saying of the good news, and it may be part of the narration reported in the Qur'an, on both possibilities. The clause is thus a concluding summary (tadhyil) indicating the totality of the excellences by which the good news was conveyed. The demonstrative is for exaltation and attention, and the pronoun of separation (huwa) is for strengthening the predicate.

The vowel of the *fatha* on "يَوْمَ" has been discussed earlier, shortly before this point.

The conjunction of "المُنافِقاتُ" to "المُنافِقُونَ" is like the conjunction of "المُؤْمِناتِ" to "المُؤْمِنِينَ" in the preceding verse.

"الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا" is a case of *taghlib* (predominance of the masculine form), because the addressees are the people of the light, and it includes both believing men and believing women.

[Page 382]

He, exalted is He, said ﴿Look at the bones, how We raise them up﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259].

*Al-intizar* (waiting) is pausing for some action. That is, "pause in your journey until we catch up with you, so that we may be illuminated by the light that is before you and beside you." This requires that God permits the first believers to proceed to Paradise in groups, while He makes the hypocrites, who were among them in Medina, walk behind them, as is reported in the hadith of intercession: "and this community will remain in it, with its hypocrites." The meaning is that they walk in darkness, so the hypocrites ask the believers to wait for them.

This is their imagined idea, so that their disappointment would be more grievous to them.

[Page 383]

then to disappoint them by setting the wall between them and the believers, because disappointment after hope is more grievous. This is mockery, which was a recompense for their mockery of the believers and their ridicule of them. *in the garrison city of Kufa, the ghoul has consumed her love.*

That is: a wall was set up between them, to confine them with it between the hypocrites and the believers. God created it at that time to cut off their hopes, and left them in darkness, unable to see. [Page 384]

The storytellers (*al-qussas*) built upon this verse fabricated interpretations concerning the virtues of the holy city of Jerusalem in Palestine, attributing them to Ka'b al-Ahbar. They named some gates of the city of Jerusalem the "Gate of Mercy," and named a place outside it the "Valley of Hell," which lies outside the wall of the city of Jerusalem. Then they applied the interpretation of the verse to these, and these are illusions upon illusions.

Know that this wall mentioned in this verse is other than the screen mentioned in Surat al-A'raf.

The pronouns in "لَهُ بابٌ", "باطِنُهُ", and "ظاهِرُهُ" refer to the wall, and the two clauses are two descriptions of "سُورٍ". The third clause is conjoined with the *waw* because the purpose of the description is the combined sense of the two conjoined clauses, as in His saying: ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

*Al-batin* is the inside of a thing, and *al-zahir* is its outside.

So *al-batin* is the inside of the wall separating the Muslims and the hypocrites, and it is the place of the Muslims.

The inwardness and outwardness here are relative, that is, with respect to the place of the Muslims and the place of the hypocrites. So the outside is the side facing the hypocrites, that is: it was set up between them with a wall from whose outside the hypocrites see the punishment that confronts them, while mercy is behind what is adjacent to them.

"قِبَلِ" with a *kasra* and then a *fatha* means the facing direction. His saying "مِن قِبَلِهِ" is a predicate placed before its subject, and "العَذابُ" is the subject, and the whole clause with its entirety is a predicate about its outside.

[Page 385]

And "مِن" has the meaning of "في" (in), like the one in His saying: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], so it is the equivalent of His saying ﴿its inside has mercy in it﴾.

*Al-'adhab* is the burning of Hell, for Hell is the abode of punishment. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed its punishment is ever adhering﴾ [al-Furqan: 65].

The clause ﴿they call out to them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from ﴿the hypocrites, men and women, say﴾.

The pronouns in ﴿they call out to them: "Were we not with you?" They said: "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, and you waited, and you doubted, and false hopes deceived you, until the command of God came, and the Deceiver deceived you concerning God"﴾ have their referents known from what preceded in His saying ﴿the day the hypocrites, men and women, say﴾, the verse.

And ﴿Were we not with you?﴾ is an *istifham taqriri* (rhetorical question seeking affirmation), used metonymically for asking to catch up with them and join them, as they were with them in the world, doing the deeds of Islam among the Muslims.

*Al-ma'iyya* (being with) was applied to participation in the deeds of Islam, such as uttering the word of Islam and performing its acts of worship. They imagined that treatment in the Hereafter proceeds as treatment in this world, according to the forms of deeds, and they did not realize that the forms are complementary, and that their foundation is sincerity of faith. This reply is an acknowledgment that the hypocrites used to do their deeds with them.

Since this acknowledgment could give the impression that it is an answer in accordance with the rhetorical question, they followed their acknowledging reply with a *istidrak* (corrective addition) that removes what the hypocrites had imagined: that agreement with the believers in the deeds of Islam is enough to join them in the bliss of Paradise. So they explained to them the causes of their separation, namely that their inner state was contrary to their outer appearance.

They mentioned to them four principles, which are the causes of loss: the temptation of their own souls, waiting for the believers, doubt about the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), and being deluded by what their own souls embellish for them.

These four are the principal roots of the traits that branch from hypocrisy.

The first: their temptation of themselves, that is, the lack of settledness of their consciences upon Islam. So in their doubt they waver, as if instability and lack of steadiness were a trait of theirs. When good thoughts of faith and love for the believers arise in their souls, they undo them with thoughts of disbelief and hatred, and this is of the making of their own souls. So the ascription of the temptations to them is a real ascription, and likewise is the case with their deeds, such as prayer and charity.

[Page 386]

This arises from lying, deception, mockery, and disparagement of the Muslims. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They wish to take their disputes to the tyrant, though they were commanded to reject him﴾ [al-Nisa': 60].

The second: waiting (*al-tarabbus*). *Al-tarabbus* is awaiting something, and it was discussed in His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], the verse.

Its verb takes an object directly, and what goes beyond the object is connected to it with "بِـ". Here he omitted its object and its complement, so as to include the many matters the hypocrites await concerning the believers, and these are many, and their return is to harming the believers and injuring them. So they await the defeat of the Muslims in the battles and similar events. He, exalted is He, said concerning some of them: ﴿and they wait for misfortunes to befall you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98]. And they await the division of the believers. They said to a group of the Ansar, to make them regret those among their people who were killed in some of the battles: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168].

The third: doubt about the religion, which is uncertainty about relying on the people of Islam or on the disbelievers, and from it arises abstention from jihad. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they are in their doubt, wavering﴾ [al-Tawbah: 45]. For this reason they did not believe in fixed appointed terms, and they said to their brethren: ﴿If they had stayed with us, they would not have died, nor been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156].

The fourth: being deluded by false hopes. *Al-amani* is the plural of *umniyya*, which is the noun of wishing. What is meant by it is what they wished for themselves: that they were upon the truth, that the victory of the believers is a passing accident, and that events proceed according to their desire and their whim. Among this is their saying: ﴿Surely the mightier will drive out the meaner from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], and their saying: ﴿If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167]. For this reason they think the outcome will be theirs: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. I have already explained the traits that arise from hypocrisy in my tafsir of Surat al-Baqarah, so apply these four principles to it, and attach the branches of some of them to others.

The purpose of the limit expressed by ﴿until the command of God came﴾ is to censure them: that they did not desist from their error despite the long duration of their lives and the succession of years upon them, while they did not reflect on the outcomes, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed?﴾ [Fatir: 37]. The ascription of the change to the false hopes is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), because the false hopes and the greed for their fulfilment are the cause of their delusion and what accompanies it.

The coming of the command of God is death, that is, until they are finished in that evil state, and did not turn away from it with true faith.

The clause of purpose (al-ghayah) is placed between the two conjoined clauses. It is incumbent upon the believer to take a lesson from what His saying, the Exalted, contains: ﴿And false hopes deceived you until the Command of Allah came﴾, and so on. Therefore he does not procrastinate in repentance, nor say, "Tomorrow, tomorrow."

The clause ﴿And the Deceiver deceived you concerning Allah﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿And false hopes deceived you﴾. This belittles their delusion and their hopes by declaring them to be from the scheming of Shaytan (Satan), so that they will increase in regret at that time.

What is meant is Shaytan, that is, by his casting thoughts of hypocrisy into their souls, dressing them in the garb of truth and in pleasing the religion of disbelief, which they claim is pleased with them: ﴿And they say, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 20].

It is also possible that what is meant is the class of deceivers, that is: "And the leaders of disbelief and the commanders of hypocrisy deceived you concerning Allah."

Al-taghrir (deception) is the presenting of harm in the form of benefit, through disguise and sophistry.
