So *al-batin* is the inside of the wall separating the Muslims and the hypocrites, and it is the place of the Muslims.

The inwardness and outwardness here are relative, that is, with respect to the place of the Muslims and the place of the hypocrites. So the outside is the side facing the hypocrites, that is: it was set up between them with a wall from whose outside the hypocrites see the punishment that confronts them, while mercy is behind what is adjacent to them.

"قِبَلِ" with a *kasra* and then a *fatha* means the facing direction. His saying "مِن قِبَلِهِ" is a predicate placed before its subject, and "العَذابُ" is the subject, and the whole clause with its entirety is a predicate about its outside.

[Page 385]

And "مِن" has the meaning of "في" (in), like the one in His saying: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], so it is the equivalent of His saying ﴿its inside has mercy in it﴾.

*Al-'adhab* is the burning of Hell, for Hell is the abode of punishment. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed its punishment is ever adhering﴾ [al-Furqan: 65].

The clause ﴿they call out to them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from ﴿the hypocrites, men and women, say﴾.

The pronouns in ﴿they call out to them: "Were we not with you?" They said: "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, and you waited, and you doubted, and false hopes deceived you, until the command of God came, and the Deceiver deceived you concerning God"﴾ have their referents known from what preceded in His saying ﴿the day the hypocrites, men and women, say﴾, the verse.

And ﴿Were we not with you?﴾ is an *istifham taqriri* (rhetorical question seeking affirmation), used metonymically for asking to catch up with them and join them, as they were with them in the world, doing the deeds of Islam among the Muslims.

*Al-ma'iyya* (being with) was applied to participation in the deeds of Islam, such as uttering the word of Islam and performing its acts of worship. They imagined that treatment in the Hereafter proceeds as treatment in this world, according to the forms of deeds, and they did not realize that the forms are complementary, and that their foundation is sincerity of faith. This reply is an acknowledgment that the hypocrites used to do their deeds with them.

Since this acknowledgment could give the impression that it is an answer in accordance with the rhetorical question, they followed their acknowledging reply with a *istidrak* (corrective addition) that removes what the hypocrites had imagined: that agreement with the believers in the deeds of Islam is enough to join them in the bliss of Paradise. So they explained to them the causes of their separation, namely that their inner state was contrary to their outer appearance.

They mentioned to them four principles, which are the causes of loss: the temptation of their own souls, waiting for the believers, doubt about the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), and being deluded by what their own souls embellish for them.

These four are the principal roots of the traits that branch from hypocrisy.

The first: their temptation of themselves, that is, the lack of settledness of their consciences upon Islam. So in their doubt they waver, as if instability and lack of steadiness were a trait of theirs. When good thoughts of faith and love for the believers arise in their souls, they undo them with thoughts of disbelief and hatred, and this is of the making of their own souls. So the ascription of the temptations to them is a real ascription, and likewise is the case with their deeds, such as prayer and charity.

[Page 386]

This arises from lying, deception, mockery, and disparagement of the Muslims. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They wish to take their disputes to the tyrant, though they were commanded to reject him﴾ [al-Nisa': 60].

The second: waiting (*al-tarabbus*). *Al-tarabbus* is awaiting something, and it was discussed in His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], the verse.

Its verb takes an object directly, and what goes beyond the object is connected to it with "بِـ". Here he omitted its object and its complement, so as to include the many matters the hypocrites await concerning the believers, and these are many, and their return is to harming the believers and injuring them. So they await the defeat of the Muslims in the battles and similar events. He, exalted is He, said concerning some of them: ﴿and they wait for misfortunes to befall you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98]. And they await the division of the believers. They said to a group of the Ansar, to make them regret those among their people who were killed in some of the battles: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168].

The third: doubt about the religion, which is uncertainty about relying on the people of Islam or on the disbelievers, and from it arises abstention from jihad. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they are in their doubt, wavering﴾ [al-Tawbah: 45]. For this reason they did not believe in fixed appointed terms, and they said to their brethren: ﴿If they had stayed with us, they would not have died, nor been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156].

The fourth: being deluded by false hopes. *Al-amani* is the plural of *umniyya*, which is the noun of wishing. What is meant by it is what they wished for themselves: that they were upon the truth, that the victory of the believers is a passing accident, and that events proceed according to their desire and their whim. Among this is their saying: ﴿Surely the mightier will drive out the meaner from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], and their saying: ﴿If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167]. For this reason they think the outcome will be theirs: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. I have already explained the traits that arise from hypocrisy in my tafsir of Surat al-Baqarah, so apply these four principles to it, and attach the branches of some of them to others.

The purpose of the limit expressed by ﴿until the command of God came﴾ is to censure them: that they did not desist from their error despite the long duration of their lives and the succession of years upon them, while they did not reflect on the outcomes, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed?﴾ [Fatir: 37]. The ascription of the change to the false hopes is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), because the false hopes and the greed for their fulfilment are the cause of their delusion and what accompanies it.

The coming of the command of God is death, that is, until they are finished in that evil state, and did not turn away from it with true faith.

The clause of purpose (al-ghayah) is placed between the two conjoined clauses. It is incumbent upon the believer to take a lesson from what His saying, the Exalted, contains: ﴿And false hopes deceived you until the Command of Allah came﴾, and so on. Therefore he does not procrastinate in repentance, nor say, "Tomorrow, tomorrow."

The clause ﴿And the Deceiver deceived you concerning Allah﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿And false hopes deceived you﴾. This belittles their delusion and their hopes by declaring them to be from the scheming of Shaytan (Satan), so that they will increase in regret at that time.

Al-ghurur (the Deceiver), with a fatha on the ghayn, is an intensive form (mubalaghah) describing one who is characterized by deception. What is meant is Shaytan, that is, by his casting thoughts of hypocrisy into their souls, dressing them in the garb of truth and in pleasing the religion of disbelief, which they claim is pleased with them: ﴿And they say, "Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 20].

It is also possible that what is meant is the class of deceivers, that is: "And the leaders of disbelief and the commanders of hypocrisy deceived you concerning Allah."

Al-taghrir (deception) is the presenting of harm in the form of benefit, through disguise and sophistry.

The ba' in His saying "bi-Allah" is causal (lil-sababiyyah) or instrumental in a figurative sense (lil-alah al-majaziyyah). That is, Shaytan made the matter of Allah a cause of their deception, by imagining to them that holding to disbelief is pleasing to Allah, the Exalted, and that hypocrisy preserved for them their religion, their own souls, the dignity of their people, and gave them knowledge of the conditions of their enemy.

All of this was known to them, and they had witnessed its proofs. Because of this, they were given a consequence in His saying: ﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 15], cutting off their hope that they would be with the believers on that day as they had been with them in life.

[Page 388]

﴿Today, no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire; it is your master, and what an evil destination.﴾ This statement may be a continuation of the believers' address to the hypocrites, persisting in rebuke and reproach. This is what the exegetes have followed. The position of the conjunctive *fa'* (fa') is then clear, and the believers' knowledge that no ransom will be taken from the hypocrites and those who disbelieved comes from what they hear on that Day of the divine judgments among creation, to the extent that it has become known to the people of the gathering. Or it is knowledge firmly established in their souls from what they knew in the world of the reports of the Qur'an and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ). In that case, the conjunction in ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾ expresses what they knew in its entirety, and it is a parenthetical conjunction (*'atf mu'tarid*) prompted by the context.

It may also be a statement issued from God Most High to the hypocrites, to despair them of hoping to obtain a share of the believers' light. In that case the *fa'* is a conjunction of instruction (*'atf al-talqin*), conjoining one speaker's words to another's for the sake of the unity of the place of address, in the manner of His saying, ﴿He said, "And from my offspring"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124].

The conjunction of ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾ would then be a gathering of the two groups under a single rebuke and reproach, since they are united in disbelief.

The insertion of the word "*fa-al-yawma*" (today) serves to remind them of what they used to conceal in the world when they spent alongside the believers, out of show and dissimulation. This is what God related of them in His saying, ﴿And among the desert Arabs are those who take what they spend as a penalty, and wait for misfortunes to befall you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98].

The majority read *lā yu'khadhu* with the *yā'* of the third-person masculine, because the feminine gender of *fidyah* is not real, and the verb has been separated from its subject by the adverbial phrase, so there are two justifications for omitting the feminine marker on the verb. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read it with the *tā'* of the feminine, following the feminine gender of the subject in its wording. The two readings are equivalent.

By negating the taking of ransom, the verse alludes to the certainty of their punishment for disbelief, since they had not offered any ransom, nor was hypocrisy among the kinds of ransom. But the speech proceeds by way of metonymy (*kināya*), for it is well known that a captive or a criminal may be freed from accountability through a ransom paid on their behalf.

Thus the conjunction ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾ is intended to give the reason that there is no escape for them from the punishment of disbelief, like those who disbelieved, that is, those who openly declared disbelief until it became a state by which they were recognized. This implies that the hypocrites and the open disbelievers were together in one place at the gates of Hell. It contains a precaution against the thought that the overt disbelievers, from the implication of ﴿no ransom will be taken from you﴾, might suppose that this ruling is specific to the hypocrites, clinging to the slightest hope. Therefore the mention of ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾ is not merely a digression (*istitrad*).

*Al-ma'wa* (the refuge) is the place to which one betakes oneself, that is, one resorts to it and returns to it, and it is used as a metonymy for permanence and eternity.

This is affirmed explicitly by the clause ﴿Your refuge is the Fire﴾, meaning you return to it just as one seeking help returns to his *mawla* (master, patron) to be helped by him or to ransom himself through him. So *al-mawla* is used figuratively for the place of abode, in the manner of mockery (*tahakkum*).

It is also permissible, along with this, to make *al-mawla* the noun of place from *al-wali* (proximity, nearness), meaning your place of abode, as in the verse of Labid:

*Fa-ghadat kilā al-farjayni tahsabu annahu*
*mawla al-makhafati khalfuhā wa-amāmuhā*

That is: the two sides of her [the wild cow] think that the place of fear is behind her and in front of her; that is, the place of fear and its abode.

And ﴿and what an evil destination﴾ is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) that encompasses all the punishment to which they proceed. The believers may also come to know, through what they answered the people of hypocrisy, that they have arrived at the abode of realities.

[Page 390]

The commentary of Ibn ʿAshur on Surah 57, verse 16:

﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves at the remembrance of God and at what has come down of the truth, and that they should not be like those who were given the Scripture before, and the term grew long for them so their hearts became hard? And many of them are defiant wrongdoers.﴾

It is known from the opening of the commentary on this surah that this verse was revealed in Mecca in the fourth or fifth year of the mission. Muslim and others narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud that he said: "There was no time between our acceptance of Islam and the moment God admonished us with this verse, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves at the remembrance of God﴾ up to ﴿And many of them are defiant wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hadid: 26], except four years."

The intended meaning of "those who believe" is either: some of them who were falling short of the majority of believers in Mecca at that time, so God wished to awaken their hearts through this general statement, in keeping with the Qur'an's habit and the Messenger's (ﷺ) manner of indirect address, such as his saying, "What is the matter with people who do such-and-such?" and God's saying, ﴿And a group, their own selves had made them anxious, thinking about God other than the truth, the thought of the Age of Ignorance﴾ [Al ʿImran: 154]. What Ibn Masʿud said does not imply that he himself was among those whom God meant by this verse, but he feared for them out of caution and vigilance.

Thus, "those who believe" means true believers, as opposed to hypocrites who display faith, since there were no hypocrites among the Muslims in Mecca and no one was calling to hypocrisy. It is also narrated from Ibn Masʿud that when the verse was revealed, some of us began looking at one another and saying, "Have we done something new?"

Or it may be an exhortation to believers to monitor this matter and to beware of falling short.

The hamza in ﴿ألَمْ يَأْنِ﴾ (alam yaʾni, "has ... not come") is an interrogative particle used here for denial, meaning: it is denied that the time for the agent of the verb has drawn near.

It is also possible that the interrogation is for affirmation of a negation, and that the verb ﴿يَأْنِ﴾ (yaʾni) is derived from a fixed noun, al-ina, with a fatha or kasra on the hamza, meaning "the time." God says, ﴿not waiting for its ripeness﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. Close to the expression ﴿ألَمْ يَأْنِ﴾ is the common saying, "Has it not come time for you to do such-and-such?" as in the hadith of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab's conversion, where the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "Has the time not come for you, son of al-Khattab, to submit (to Islam)?" In the report of Abu Dhar's conversion, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib found him in the Sacred Mosque and wanted to host him, and said to him, "Has it not come time for the man to know his lodging?" meaning: to know my home, which is like his home. This is a gentle way of offering hospitality. However, the verb ﴿يَأْنِ﴾ is derived from al-ina, which is a defective verb whose last radical is an alif. The verb "āna" (to draw near in time) is derived from al-ayn, meaning the moment, and is a hollow verb whose last radical is a nun.

So the root of "anā, yaʾnī" is ʾ-n-y, and the root of "āna" is ʾ-w-n. The two words have the same meaning.

The lam in ﴿لِلَّذِينَ﴾ denotes cause: "has the time not come for the sake of those who believe that humbling should occur?" That is, has its presence not become due for their sake?

The clause ﴿أنْ تَخْشَعَ﴾ (an takhshaʿa, "that [their hearts] should humble themselves") is the agent of ﴿يَأْنِ﴾. Khushuʿ means submissiveness and humility.

﴿ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (dhikr Allah, "the remembrance of God") refers to what the Prophet (ﷺ) reminds them of, or it may be the prayer. ﴿وما نَزَلَ مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ (wa-ma nazala min al-haqq, "and what has come down of the truth") means the Qur'an. God says, ﴿The believers are only those who, when God is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾ [al-Anfal: 2].

It is also possible that the two descriptions refer to the Qur'an, honouring it by describing it as the remembrance of God, and declaring its benefit by stating that it came down from God and that it is the truth. In that case, the statement ﴿وما نَزَلَ مِنَ الحَقِّ﴾ is an added description of the Qur'an, in the manner of the line of poetry that the author cited in al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's Qur'an commentary):

"To the lordly king and the son of al-Hammam..." [the rest of the verse].

The lam in ﴿لِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ is the lam of cause: "for the sake of the remembrance of God."

The meaning of humbling for its sake is humbling that is caused by hearing it, which is obedience and compliance.

Nafiʿ and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿وما نَزَلَ﴾ with a light zayn (nazal). The rest of the readers read it with a heavy zayn (nazzala), with the agent of nazzala understood from the context as God.

﴿ولا يَكُونُوا﴾ (wa-la yakunu, "and that they should not be") is read by the majority with the third-person yaʾ. Ruways from Yaʿqub read it as ﴿ولا تَكُونُوا﴾ (wa-la takunu) with the second-person taʾ.

According to the majority reading, the la is a negation particle, and the verb is governed by the preceding infinitival an, and the sense is: "Has the time not come for them that they should not be like those who were given the Scripture?" According to Ruways' reading from Yaʿqub, the taʾ of address is an iltifat (a shift from third to second person), and la is a negation particle, and the verb is in the subjunctive by coordination, as in the majority reading. Or la may be a prohibitive particle, the verb is in the jussive, and the coordination is coordination of clauses.

The purpose is warning, but they had already become involved in that, and it was not yet time for them to desist from it. The warning is directed at what happened to the People of the Book: the hardening of hearts after the long period during which they practised their religion. That is, let those who believe beware lest they become like them while they are still newly acquainted with the religion. The intent is not to give an excuse to the People of the Book for the long period that passed over them, because a long period is not a cause of negligence in what it lasted over. Rather, the matter is the reverse. Nor is the intent to minimise the occurrence of this for those who believe after a long period has passed, because that does not bear on the purpose before the long period. The intent is rather to forbid imitating those who were given the Scripture in failing to humble their hearts. But it also conveys a warning to believers, after a long time has passed, that they should not fall into what the People of the Book fell into. This entails the information that the period of the Muslims will soon last as long as, or longer than, the period of the People of the Book who were before the mission, since the Qur'an is an admonition for ages and generations.

It is also possible to take la as a prohibitive particle, with the prohibition directed at the third person by iltifat, or the meaning being: "Convey to them that they should not be."

The fa in ﴿فَطالَ عَلَيْهِمُ الأمَدُ﴾ (fa-ṭala ʿalayhimu al-amad, "and the term grew long for them") is the fa of consequence, presenting the length of the period as following from the hardening of hearts through lack of humility. This consequence lies outside the comparison in God's words ﴿like those who were given the Scripture before﴾, but it is an alert to the outcome of that comparison, as a warning that there may befall them what befell those who were given the Scripture before.

Al-amad means the limit or extent, whether of place or of time. Here it means the period during which they were charged to preserve the observance of their laws, which was limited by the coming of the Messenger (ﷺ), who was foretold in the laws. God says, ﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then a messenger will come to you confirming what is with you; you must believe in him and support him"﴾ [Al ʿImran: 81].

The meaning is: they forgot what they had been charged with, opposed the rulings of their laws, and did not fear God's punishment. They took the lowly gain of this world and said, "We will be forgiven," so they cast it behind their backs and bartered it for a price. This became their habit little by little, until they became accustomed to it, and so their hearts hardened, that is, they became rebellious in daring to change the rulings of the religion.

The clause ﴿وكَثِيرٌ مِنهم فاسِقُونَ﴾ (wa-kathirun minhum fasiqun, "and many of them are defiant wrongdoers") is a parenthetical clause at the end of the statement.

The meaning is: many of them went beyond that limit of hardening of hearts, so they rejected their religion, altered their Scripture and distorted it, corrupted their beliefs, and thus reached the limit of disbelief. So fisq here means disbelief, as in God's words, ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us only because we believed in God and in what was sent down to us and what was sent down before, and because most of you are defiant wrongdoers?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59]. That is, they were not believers, as indicated by the contrast with the words ﴿we believed in God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59] and what follows.

Between the word ﴿فَقَسَتْ﴾ (faqasat, "became hard") and the word ﴿فاسِقُونَ﴾ (fasiqun, "defiant wrongdoers") there is a jinas (paronomasia, a figure of speech based on similar-sounding words) that adds beauty to the expression. This type is composed of what is called jinas al-qalb (metathetical paronomasia, where the same letters appear in reversed order) and what is called jinas al-naqis (defective paronomasia, where the two words differ by one letter), and both are combined in this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 17:

﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death. We have certainly made the signs clear to you, that you may understand.﴾

The opening of speech with "i‘lamū" (know) and similar expressions indicates that what follows deserves the full attention of the mind, as was explained earlier at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235], in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, a fifth of it is for Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], the verse in Surat al-Anfal.

Here it points out that the statement which follows carries a great meaning that is not apparent, for it is intended to depict the state of believing hearts in their need of the remembrance of Allah by the state of dead earth in its need of rain, and the state of remembrance in purifying souls and illuminating them by the state of the rain in reviving barren land. This is indicated by His saying after it, ﴿We have certainly made the signs clear to you, that you may understand﴾. Otherwise, Allah's reviving of the earth after its death through the rain that reaches it is not hidden, so it does not require that the report about it begin with something like "i‘lamū" unless it carries an unusual indication, namely the indication of parable (tamthīl). A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu Mas‘ud al-Badri, when he saw him strike the face of a slave of his: "Know, Abu Mas‘ud, know, Abu Mas‘ud, that Allah is more able to exercise power over you than you are over this [slave]."

So the sentence stands in the position of a reason for the sentence ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah?﴾ [al-Hadid: 16] up to His saying "and their hearts hardened," because that sentence contains an exhortation to humility

Page 394
before the remembrance of Allah. But this sentence is in the position of a cause and is separated (fuṣilat) and not joined by a conjunction (lam tu‘taf). This requires that it was revealed together with His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves﴾ [al-Hadid: 16], the verse.

The address in His saying "i‘lamū" to the believers is in the manner of iltifat (shift of address), turning toward them for the sake of emphasis.

His saying ﴿that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾ is a clear parabolic metaphor (isti‘ara tamthiliyya musarraha), and it contains an implicit parabolic metaphor (tamthiliyya makniyya) because it includes the comparison of the state of the remembrance of Allah and the Qur'an in reforming hearts with the state of rain in reforming the earth after its drought. The state being compared to (al-hala al-mushabbah bihā) was omitted, and it was alluded to by its necessary concomitant, which is the attribution of the reviving of the earth to Allah, because Allah gives life to the earth after its death by means of rain, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah sends down water from the sky, and with it He gives life to the earth after its death?﴾

The purpose is to guide toward the means of turning in repentance to Allah, to urge care for the soul through admonition, and to remind of turning to the Qur'an, reflecting upon it, and the words of the Messenger (ﷺ) and his teaching; and that in seeking refuge in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ) there is salvation, and in turning to both of them there is protection. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have left among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah and my Sunnah." He also said: "The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which Allah sent me is like abundant rain that fell upon a land; part of it was fertile, which absorbed the water and produced grass and herbage; and part of it was hard ground that held water, so Allah benefited people with it, and they drank, gave drink, and cultivated. And it fell upon another part, which was barren plains that neither hold water nor produce vegetation. That is the likeness of one who comprehends the religion of Allah and benefits from what Allah sent me with, so he knows and teaches; and the likeness of one who does not raise his head to that and does not accept the guidance of Allah with which I was sent."

His saying ﴿We have certainly made the signs clear to you, that you may understand﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani) relative to the sentence ﴿that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾, because the hearer of His saying ﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾ seeks to know the purpose of this informing, so His saying ﴿We have certainly made the signs clear to you﴾ is an answer to his seeking, meaning: We have informed you of this as a making clear of the signs.

By its generality it conveys the function of a concluding summary (tadhyil) for the preceding verses from the beginning of the surah, both Meccan and Medinan, because

Page 395
although this verse is Medinan, its placement after the verses revealed in Mecca is intended by Allah, the Exalted, and the command to place it in this position indicates that; and because the definite article in "the signs" (al-ayat) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq), as is the case with the definite plural with al-.

"Al-ayat" means the proofs (al-dala'il). What is meant by them includes the content of His saying ﴿and do not be like those who were given the Book before, and the term grew long for them﴾ [al-Hadid: 16] up to His saying "after its death," and this is the place of coining a parable, because the comparison with the state of the People of the Book is a form of parabolic illustration.

The making clear of the signs is achieved through the eloquence and rhetorical excellence of the speech, the abundance of its meanings, and their clarification, and all of this is present in these verses as you have known just now. Among the clearest forms of explanation is comparison with the states of those who are similar, in the context of warning or exhortation.

"La‘allakum ta‘qilūn" (that you may understand) expresses hope and causation, meaning: We have made it clear to you because your state is like that of one whose understanding is hoped for, and the clarification is the cause of his understanding.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who lend to Allah a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward.﴾

It seems likely that this verse is Medinan (al-Madani, "from the Medinan period") and that its meaning is connected to His saying, ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He multiplies it for him, and he will have a noble reward?﴾ [al-Hadid: 11]. The verse ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe...﴾ [al-Hadid: 16] and what follows it is an interjection (i'tiraD). The Meccan (al-Makki) and Medinan verses are interwoven with one another in this surah. Do you not see that the wording of the two verses is similar, since the intention is to repeat what preceded of exhortation to spending, so it is presented in the form of the attribute by which those who comply with that exhortation are known?

He conjoined "wa al-Musaddiqat" (and the women who give charity) as he did before in His saying, ﴿The day you see the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Hadid: 12], and because stinginess is more common among women, as the poetry of the Arabs indicates.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read "wa al-Musaddiqin" with the shadda on the ṣād, on the basis that its original form is al-mutasaddiqin. The tā' was assimilated (idgham) into the ṣād after being converted into a ṣād, because the two points of articulation are close, seeking the lightness of assimilation. Thus His saying ﴿and lent to Allah a goodly loan﴾ is a conjunction of something synonymous in meaning with what is in the conjoined term, because it likens their act to a loan to Allah, as an honouring of acts of charity.

Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read it with the ṣād unshadda, on the basis that it derives from al-taṣdiq (affirmation), i.e., those who affirmed the Messenger ﷺ, meaning: they believed and complied with his command, so they lent to Allah a goodly loan.

The majority read "yuḍā'af lahum" with an alif after the ḍād. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "yuḍa''af" without an alif and with the shadda on the 'ayn.

"Wa aqraḍū" is conjoined, and it is a full clause, to "al-Musaddiqin," which is a singular noun phrase, because the noun phrase is in the position of a verb, since the lam (in al-Musaddiqin) carries the meaning of a relative pronoun. So the force of the speech is: "Indeed, those men who gave charity, and those women who gave charity, and [they] lent," by way of taghlib (predominance of the masculine). There is no intervening foreign element, and an intervening element is not prohibited when it does not corrupt the meaning.

The reason for departing from parallel construction of the two relative clauses, so that it is not said "Indeed, the charitable men and the lending men," is to depict the meaning that giving charity is itself a lending to Allah.

The meaning of ﴿It will be multiplied for them, and they will have a noble reward﴾ has already been explained in His saying, ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan so that He multiplies it for him﴾ [al-Hadid: 11], and so on.

[Page 397]

When the virtue of those who give charity was mentioned, and some believers have no wealth from which to give charity, he followed the mention of those who give charity with an explanation of the virtue of believers in general. This includes both those who are able to give charity and those who are not, in the manner of the earlier reminder in His words ﴿And to each God has promised the best﴾ [Al-Hadid: 10].

In a hadith: "Some of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'O Messenger of God, the people of abundant wealth have taken the rewards. They pray as we pray, fast as we fast, and give charity from the surplus of their wealth, while we have no wealth.' He said: 'Has God not made for you that with which you may give charity? Indeed, for each tasbih (glorification of God) there is a charity, for each tahmid (praise of God) a charity, for each takbir (proclamation of God's greatness) a charity, enjoining good is a charity, and forbidding evil is a charity.'"

"Those who believe" (al-ladhina amanu) encompasses everyone to whom the content of this relative clause and what is conjoined to it applies.

In the plural "and His messengers" (wa rusulihi) there is an allusion to the People of the Book, who said: "We believe in some and disbelieve in others." The Jews believed in God and in Musa (Moses), but disbelieved in 'Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. The Christians believed in God but disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). The believers believed in all of God's messengers, and for this reason they are described as ﴿the truthful ones﴾ (al-siddiqun).

Al-siddiq (the truthful one, the one of exceptional sincerity), with the letter dal doubled, is an intensive form of the one who affirms, like al-misik for the stingy, meaning one who holds tightly to his wealth. The more common pattern is derived from the triliteral root, as in al-dilil. It may also be derived from the augmented forms, because the less frequently used patterns are given more latitude, as the form al-sami' is used in the sense of "the one who makes hear" in the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib, and al-hakim is used in the sense of "the one who judges" among the Names of God. They were described as truthful because they affirmed all the true messengers, and no partisanship or obstinacy prevented them from doing so. The description of Yusuf as siddiq has already been mentioned in the Surah of Yusuf, and Maryam is described as siddiqa in Surah al-Ma'idah.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), "hum" in ﴿they are the truthful ones﴾, indicates restriction (qasr), and it is a restriction relative to a specific context: they are the truthful ones, not those who denied some of the messengers. This negates the possibility that the People of the Book could be truthful, since their affirmation of their messenger has no benefit when they did not affirm the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The demonstrative pronoun (ism al-ishara) serves to honour their status and to draw attention to the fact that those referred to deserved what follows the demonstrative because of the qualities that precede it.

* * *

﴿And the martyrs, with their Lord, for them is their reward and their light﴾.

It is permissible for this to be conjoined to "the truthful ones" (al-siddiqun), as a conjunction of a singular noun to a singular noun, so it is a conjunction to the predicate, meaning: "and they are the martyrs." This interpretation is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, Zayd ibn Aslam, and a group of others. It is said that the meaning of their being martyrs is that they are witnesses over the nations on the Day of Recompense, as He says ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 143]. Thus the testimony (shahada) here means a report that establishes a right, for which one is recompensed with good or evil.

It was also said that its meaning is that the believers of this Ummah are like the martyrs of the nations, that is, like their slain in the way of God. This is reported from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

In this case the clause ﴿with their Lord, for them is their reward and their light﴾ is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), arising from the description of them with these two attributes, since the listener anticipates what their reward is from these two virtues.

It is also permissible for "and the martyrs" (wa al-shuhada') to be the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿with their Lord, for them is their reward and their light﴾ is the predicate of the subject. The conjunction is then a conjunction of sentences (min 'atf al-jumal), and one pauses at "the truthful ones" (al-siddiqun). This interpretation is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, and al-Dahhak. In this case it is a transition from describing the virtue of faith in God and His Messenger (ﷺ) to describing the virtue of a group among them who singled out the excellence of martyrdom in the way of God. This is part of the continuation of His words ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of God﴾ [Al-Hadid: 10] up to His words ﴿And God is Aware of what you do﴾ [Al-Hadid: 10]. When He had emphasised the promise to the believers who affirm, the unburdened ones, from His words ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in God, while the Messenger calls you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 8], etc., He then fulfilled their right with His words ﴿Those who believe in God and His messengers, those are the truthful ones﴾, and turned to the promise to the martyrs in the way of God, whose mention is contained in His words ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of God﴾ [Al-Hadid: 10] and the verses that follow. So the martyrs are then those who were slain in jihad in the way of God.

The two meanings of "martyrs" can be combined, so the verse may be understood as intending both, in the manner of the usage of the shared term (mushtarak) in both of its meanings. We have established in many places that the Qur'an uses words in this way.

The pronouns in "their reward" (ajruhum) and "their light" (nuruhum) refer either to the truthful ones and the martyrs, or to the martyrs alone, according to the two views previously mentioned regarding the conjunction.

"With their Lord" (inda rabbihim) is connected to the stable element (al-istiqrar) within the prepositional phrase that is the predicate of the subject. The implied meaning is: "for them their reward is established with their Lord." The "with" (indiyya) is metaphorical, used for care and favour.

The apparent sense of the pronoun's reference is that it refers to something mentioned in the wording with its mentioned meaning. The apparent meaning of "their reward and their light" is that it is the reward of those mentioned, and the attribution of reward and light to their pronoun means that it is a reward by which they are made known and a light by which they are made known.

Since the function of an attributive construction (idafa) is to define the first term by its relation to the second, and since the reward and light were unknown to the listener, the speech contains a vagueness by which is expressed a great reward and a great light. It is therefore an allusion to honouring that reward and that light, meaning: a reward and a light that cannot be described except as "their reward and their light," that is, a reward and light fitting for a station, together with what the "with" in "with their Lord" conveys of nearness and care for them, which implies great reward and light.

It is also permissible for the two pronouns in "their reward and their light" to refer to the terms "the truthful ones" and "the martyrs," or to the term "the martyrs" alone, according to what has preceded, but with a meaning other than the one previously assigned. Rather, it refers to the truthful ones and the martyrs among those who came before them from the earlier nations. This is what al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf.

The meaning of the truthful ones and the martyrs in this case differs from the earlier meaning in generality and specificity, following the method of istikhdam (using a word in one sense and its pronoun in another) in the pronoun. It also follows the method of the eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), in which the predicate is attributed to the subject in His words ﴿for them is their reward and their light﴾, with the implied meaning: "for them is the like of their reward and their light." There is no need for interpretation in the attribution of reward and light to the two pronouns on this interpretation, since the definiteness of the attributive term is clear, because it is established among people that the truthful ones and the martyrs of the earlier nations were promised it. God said concerning them ﴿and they were witnesses over it﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 44], and He said ﴿Those are with those whom God has blessed, of the prophets, the truthful ones, the martyrs, and the righteous, and excellent are those as companions﴾ [Al-Nisa': 69].

The benefit of the simile in this way is to portray the strength of the one compared, even if it is stronger than the thing to which it is compared, because the past states have a fame and certainty that bring the image of the one compared close to the addressee. Among this is what is in the wording of the prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ), with the simile in His words "as You prayed upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim."

* * *

﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾.

This is a completion required by the mention of the people of the degrees of faith and the honouring of them. He then followed that with the description of

[Page 400]

their opposites, because that increases the honouring of them, as their faith saved them from the Blazing Fire.

By "those who disbelieved" is meant those who disbelieved in God and denied the Qur'an, which includes the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians, with variation among them in the levels of the Fire. The polytheists deserved the Fire for all aspects of their disbelief. The Jews deserved it from the day they denied 'Isa (peace be upon him). Some Christians deserved it when they ascribed a son to God, and some from the time they denied the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Introducing them with the definite demonstrative (ism al-ishara) indicates that they are deserving of this because of disbelief and denial, similar to what preceded in His words ﴿those are the truthful ones﴾. The pronoun of separation was not used in their predicate, since it is not supposed that anyone other than them are the companions of the Blazing Fire.

Expressing them as "companions of" (ashab), in an attributive construction with "the Blazing Fire" (al-jahim), indicates the intensity of their close attachment to the Blazing Fire.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 20 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and diversion, adornment and boasting among you, and rivalry in wealth and children.﴾

He follows the exhortation to charity and spending with a pointer to removing the cause of stinginess (shuhh), which is greed for keeping wealth in order to spend it on the pleasures of this worldly life. So the life of this world is presented to them through a belittling image, to show that it is transient, to belittle what is attained in it, and to make them averse to it, because attachment to it prevents success. God Almighty said: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.﴾ [al-Hashr: 9] And He said: ﴿And souls have been made present with stinginess. But if you do good and fear God, then indeed God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ [al-Nisa': 128]

All of this is in the context of urging spending, both obligatory and otherwise. It is indicated that life should be taken as a means to lasting bliss in the Hereafter and as a protection from severe punishment. Apart from that, the other conditions of life are little enjoyment. For this reason, after the image of the life of this world, He followed with information about the Hereafter, by His saying: ﴿And in the Hereafter there is a severe punishment﴾, and so on.

The opening of this with His saying "Know" (i'lamu) is for the reason I explained a moment ago regarding His saying: ﴿Know that God gives life to the earth after its death﴾ [al-Hadid: 17].

The "annama" with an open hamza is a sister of "innama" with a kasra on the hamza in conveying restriction (al-hasr). The restriction of the life of this world in the reports about it is the restriction of people's conditions in life to these six matters, with regard to the majority of people. It is therefore a claimed (ida'i) restriction, judged by what the aspirations of most people turn toward among the affairs of the worldly life. Those who are free of some of these may not be free of involvement in others, except for those whom God Most High protected, so that He made their actions in all of life for the sake of God. Otherwise, life may include acts of piety, benefits, kindness, support for the truth, teaching of virtues, and enacting of laws.

Here are mentioned the affairs of life that most people are generally given to, and that which does not escape from the lapse of wasting noble goals or plunging into blameworthy faults. These are also the basic states of the society's life, and they are also the basic phases of the individual lives of people in each one's development. Play is the phase of childhood and youth; diversion is the phase of young manhood; adornment is the phase of vigor; boasting is the phase of middle age; and rivalry is the phase of old age. Five things are mentioned here.

As for play (la'ib): it is a name for a speech or act intended for joking and levity, to pass the time, or to relieve the loneliness of solitude, or stillness, or silence, or to bring joy and pleasure to the soul, or it brings the like to the beloved, or it brings its opposite to the hateful. Examples are moving the limbs and shaking them to ward off the loneliness of stillness, and purposeless babbling to ward off the loneliness of silence. Among it is frivolity, and like joking with a woman to attract her attention, or with a child out of affection or to please him.

Play is what predominates in the activities of infants and young boys. The phase of childhood is the phase of play. Others vary in how much they engage in it: it decreases or increases according to the differences among people in the early phases of human life, and in the soundness or weakness of their minds. Excess in it by those who are beyond its phase indicates baseness of mind. For this reason the people of Abraham said to him: ﴿Have you come to us with the truth, or are you of the players?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 55]

Play is common in people's conditions in this world, so it is a great part of its conditions. It is enough to know that it fills most of the conditions of childhood.

As for diversion (lahw): it is a name for an act or speech intended to gratify the soul by it and to turn it away from a pain arising from bodily fatigue, sorrow, or grief. It is said: "lahā 'an al-shay'" meaning he occupied himself with it, distracted himself from it. Imru' al-Qays said:

*And a veiled maiden whose tent is not approached; I enjoyed diversion with her, not hastily.*

And al-Nabigha, mentioning his pilgrimage, said:

*May my Lord protect you. For we are not permitted the diversion of women, and the religion has resolved this.*

Diversion predominates in the conditions of youth, so the phase of youth is its phase. And diversion is abundant in worldly conditions through the pursuit of pleasures and merriment.

Adornment (zinah): it is beautifying one's self or place with what makes its appearance pleasing to the one who sees it. It is in people's nature to desire that their appearance be good in the eyes of those who look at them. This is stronger in women's nature, and perhaps among the reasons for its intensity in them is the great incitement of men toward them in this respect.

Adornment is abundant in the phase of vigor, because a man feels the beginning of the disappearance of the beauties of his youth, and a woman who used to be a beauty loves to be adorned. This is not for the sake of exposing herself to men, as men imagine about women out of self-conceit, but so that she may be pleasing to people, men and women alike.

Adornment predominates in the conditions of life, for most dwellings and clothing are intended for adornment. It is both physical and immaterial, and among the immaterial is what in the principles of jurisprudence is called "al-tahsini" (the embellishing).

Boasting (tafakhur): it is speech by which one boasts. Fakhr is a person's talk about his praiseworthy qualities and admirable attributes, whether true or false. The form of the active participle is derived from it, because the nature of boasting is that it takes place between two sides, as indicated by its restriction with the adverbial phrase "among you."

People boast of praiseworthy qualities in their eras, generations, and customs. Among the qualities, some are such that boasting of them is not false: these are the qualities whose realities are praiseworthy by reason or by the law. Among them are qualities whose boasting is false, namely qualities and deeds that a people have agreed to praise themselves for, but which do not truly deserve praise, such as boasting of inflating the price of wine, gambling, fornication, boasting of killing souls, and raiding wealth without right.

Most boasting occurs in the phase of middle age and the full maturity of strength, because it is the time of turning toward deeds intended for boasting.

Boasting is abundant in people's conditions in this world, including vanity and self-admiration, and from it arises envy.

Rivalry (takathur): it is a reciprocal form from abundance (kathrah). The reciprocal form here is for intensifying the action, to the point that it takes the place of one who competes with another in the abundance of something, for he is most eager that he have more of it than him. So a person used to look at abundance of a desired thing in the case of another person who had more of it. Do you not see the saying of Tarafah:

*Had my Lord willed, I would have been Qays ibn 'Asim, and had my Lord willed, I would have been 'Amr ibn Murthad.*

*So I became possessed of much wealth, and noble sons surrounded me, lords of the lord of his people.*

Then the use of the form "takathur" became widespread, and it came to be used for greed in acquiring much, without considering competition with others who have obtained it. God Most High said: ﴿Rivalry in abundance has distracted you﴾ [al-Takathur: 1].

The "fi" in His saying ﴿in wealth and children﴾ is either used for causality (ta'lil), or it is the figurative sense of location (al-zarfiyyah al-majaziyyah). If wealth is taken as a container, then the people's rivalry takes place within it, like one who draws water from a well.

The meaning is: God established the order of people's conditions in the worldly life on the wisdom that life be a means for souls to reach what God prepared them for, of ascending to the sublimity of kingship (al-malakiyyah), as indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am placing a successor on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. The order of this life is that people's affairs in it proceed according to the teachings of guidance, for success in eternal life, the bliss of the Truth after death and resurrection. But people have distorted it from its clear course. This is included in His saying, Most High: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾ [al-Nahl: 97].

* * *

﴿Like the example of a rain whose plants please the disbelievers; then it dries and you see it turn yellow; then it becomes debris.﴾

It may be in the position of the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is like the example of rain," so the sentence is a resumption (isti'naf). Omitting the subject of the predication is of the type that al-Sakkaki called "following usage" (mutabi'at al-isti'mal).

It may also be that the kaf is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and "kamathal" means "like the condition of": the condition of the life of this world is like the condition of rain, and so on. The state of the people of this world in their predominant conditions, and the varieties indicated by His saying "play and diversion" to the end, are compared to the image of rain that caused plants to grow, which ripened, then turned yellow, then perished and were shattered. That is, the state of these predominant conditions among people in life is compared, in being beloved to people and making them proud, and in the speed of their passing, to the state of a new plant that rain produced, which matured and became complete, and whoever saw it was impressed by it, but after a period it dried out and was shattered.

The intended subject of the image is the plant. It begins with rain to shape the image from its beginnings, to show where its beauty lies, because the thing compared gains beauty from that, as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr did in embellishing the attributes of the water with which the wine was mixed, in his saying:

*It was mixed with water of a bend-flowing spring, pure, in a valley that has become wine-bearing.*

*The winds remove its impurities, and a pure cloud pours it out, white and abundant.*

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that "al-kuffar" means "the farmers," the plural of kafir, which is the planter, because he covers the seed with the soil of the earth. "Al-kafr" with an open kaf means covering, that is, covering the seed. This name was chosen here, though God said in Surah al-Fath "it pleases the farmers," for the purpose here of an allusion (tawriyah) to the disbelievers, who are the unbelievers in God, because they are most admiring of the goods of this world, since they have no hope in anything after it. A group of commentators said: "al-kuffar" is the plural of the disbeliever in God, because they limited their admiration to deeds whose aims are worldly, to the exclusion of religious deeds. So the mention of the disbelievers is an allusion that the example is directed at them first.

"Al-nabat" is a verbal noun of "nabata." God said: ﴿And God caused you to grow from the earth a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. Here it is used for what has grown, by the use of the verbal noun for the agent, which is common. Its original purpose is intensification, and it may become widespread so that the intention of intensification disappears from it.

As for His saying "then it dries" (thumma yahiju): the commentators' statements agreed on interpreting "yahiju" as "it dries out" or "becomes parched," but they did not cite evidence from Arabic speech showing that one of the meanings of "hiyaj" is dryness. Al-Raghib said: "It is said: 'hāja al-baql' (the herbage dried), when it turned yellow and became good." In al-Asas: "Metaphorically, 'hāja al-baql' when it began to become dry." These two imams did not make "hāja" mean "yabisa" (dried up). How could they, given the wording of the verse ﴿then it dries, and you see it yellow﴾? The correct view is that "hiyaj" is coarseness and approaching dryness, because the root of "hiyaj" indicates agitation and turmoil, and war is called "al-hayja'" (the battle). Al-Nabigha said:

*Did the abodes of the traces of Su'da stir you?*

When the crop becomes coarse, its movement produces a sound, so it seems agitated, that is, stirring, and that is the beginning of its drying. This is like His saying, Most High: ﴿like a seed that sends out its shoot, then strengthens it, and it becomes thick and stands on its stalk, pleasing the farmers﴾ [al-Fath: 29], in Surah al-Fath.

The clause "yahiju" is conjoined with "thumma" to indicate a rank-based sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutabi), because the yellowing of the plant is the greatest indication of readiness for disappearance, and this is what matters most in the context of renouncing the goods of this world.

He conjoined "then you see it yellow" with "fa" (then) because the yellowing of the plant is close to its drying out. And conjoining "thumma yakunu hutaman" (then it becomes debris) with "thumma" is like conjoining "thumma yahiju."

Al-hutam, with a damma on the ha', is what has been shattered, that is, broken into pieces.

So He presented the image of the life of this world through the stages of what is in it: youth, middle age, old age, then perishing; and newness, then decay, then decrepitude; and the coming of affairs at the time of their coming, then their receding afterward, through the stages of the crop. All of these are transient accidents, and their end is perishing.

And the stages of a person's life mentioned in His saying "play and diversion" through "and children" are included in it, as becomes apparent upon reflection.

This illustration, although it is a comparison of a composite state with a similar state, is suitable for detailed distribution, with each part of the compared state matched against the corresponding part of the state used as the comparison. Thus, the first stages of life and its approach are likened to plant growth following rain; those who benefit from the approach of worldly prosperity are likened to farmers; the completion of life's conditions and the strength of middle age are likened to the flourishing of the crop; the beginning of old age, then decrepitude, and the beginning of the weakening of the worker's labour, the trader's trade, and the farmer's husbandry, are likened to the yellowing of the crop and its readiness for perishing; and the loss of whatever strength and wealth a person had is likened to the crushing of the crop.

It is understood from this that whatever of life's conditions is intended for the sake of God's countenance belongs to the matters of the Hereafter, and therefore does not fall under this illustration except outwardly. Acts of righteousness, the study of knowledge, and the like are not afflicted by deficiency as long as their doer is devoted to them, and some of them increase in growth with the passage of time. A parallel to this verse has preceded in Surat al-Zumar.

* * *

﴿And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment, and forgiveness from God and good pleasure, while the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.﴾

The mention of the state of the worldly life called for the mention of a contrast, according to the Qur'an's custom, and the statement is used for warning and encouragement, as indicated by the context. For this reason, it did not specify the people of punishment and the people of forgiveness and good pleasure, since that is evident.

Bliss is expressed by "forgiveness from God and good pleasure," because bliss is of two kinds: material and spiritual. Forgiveness and good pleasure are the root of spiritual bliss, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And good pleasure from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]. These two necessitate physical bliss, because when the people of Paradise have their essences composed of bodies and spirits are deposited in them, the two kinds of bliss are fitting for them, multiplying pleasures; and the pleasure of bodies is nothing but what reaches the spirits, since it is they that perceive pleasures. God's good pleasure necessitates giving them the furthest extent of that by which they find delight, and His forgiveness necessitates pardoning whatever might hinder some of that.
