There are other aspects to it, which we will not lengthen with.

By "those who are stingy" is meant the hypocrites. Allah described them with a similar attribute in Surat al-Nisa'. Their enjoining people to stinginess is what Allah related of them in His words, ﴿They are those who say: Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7], that is, upon the believers.

The clause ﴿And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ is a concluding generalizing statement (tadhyil), because "whoever turns away" encompasses those who are stingy and others. Indeed, ﴿those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾, that is, in the way of Allah and in obligatory expenditures, have turned away from the command of Allah. And "man" (whoever) is a general conditional particle.

[Page 414]

The clause ﴿indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ stands in the place of the response of the conditional clause, because its content is the reason for the response. Thus the estimation is: and whoever turns away, then he does not harm Allah at all, nor does he harm the poor, because Allah is free of need of the wealth of those who turn away, and because He has servants who obey His command, so He praises them.

Al-Ghani (the Free of need): the one described with independence, that is, non-need. Since no object is mentioned for it, it conveys general independence.

Al-Hamid: an intensive form (sifat mubalaghah), that is, one who praises the spenders abundantly, in the manner of His words, ﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion, Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], and so on.

Describing Him here as "al-Hamid" is the counterpart of describing Him as "al-Shakur" in His words, ﴿If you lend to Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you. And Allah is Appreciative and Forbearing﴾ [al-Taghabun: 17]. Indeed His name "al-Hamid" is suitable for the meaning of "the praised" (mahmud), so it is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), and it is suitable for the meaning of "one who praises abundantly," so it is one of the forms of intensification, because Allah rewards the doing of good with a great reward and praises its doer with a beautiful commendation, so by that He is one who praises abundantly. Ibn Barrajan al-Ishbili adopted both meanings in his commentary on the Most Beautiful Names of Allah, and the words of Ibn al-'Arabi in Ahkam al-Qur'an in Surat al-A'raf agree with him, and this is the truth. Al-Ghazali, however, restricted it in al-Maqsad al-Asna to the meaning of "the praised."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far recited ﴿indeed Allah, the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ without a separating pronoun (damir fasl), and so it is written in the Madinan and Syrian codices. The rest recited ﴿indeed Allah, He is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ with a separating pronoun after the name of Majesty (Allah), and so it is written in the codices of Makkah, Basra and Kufa. Thus these are two mutawatir (mass-transmitted) readings.

[Page 415]

The sentence, without a separating pronoun, conveys restriction (qasr), because defining the subject and the predicate is one of the means of restriction. So the recitation with the separating pronoun conveys the emphasis of the restriction.

[Page 416]

This is a fresh resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a sentence that begins a new thought while following on from what precedes it) arising from what came before: the exhortation to spend in the way of Allah and concerning the conquest, and the concluding remark of that passage, His saying ﴿And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Hadid: 24]. It is a warning to the hypocrites who turn away, so that they may make amends for their condition by following the Messenger ﷺ and reflecting upon the guidance of the Qur'an. It is also a threat to them that if they do not refrain and submit to the manifest proof, their crookedness will be straightened by sharp swords. This is what He made explicit to them in His saying in Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿If the hypocrites do not desist, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in the city, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors therein except briefly﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60], ﴿Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with [severe] slaying﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61], and in His saying in Surat al-Tahrim: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh upon them﴾ [al-Tahrim: 9]. This is so that they do not think that His saying ﴿And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Hadid: 24] is merely abandonment, and thus feel secure in that.

The emphasis of the statement by the lam of oath and the particle of certainty (*harf al-tahqiq*) refers to what the statement contains concerning what is in the sending of Allah's messengers and His books, namely the establishment of justice among people, and to an allusion to subduing those who turn away by the sword if they persist in their arrogance.

The plural "*al-Rusul*" (the messengers) here serves to convey that what Muhammad ﷺ brought is not an innovation among the messengers, and that the obstinacy of the hypocrites is blindness to the way (*sunnah*) of Allah in His creation. The emphasis on this is built upon treating the listeners as though they were those who deny that Allah sent messengers before Muhammad ﷺ, because their state in marvelling at his claim to prophethood is like the state of one who denies that Allah sent messengers before. A similar expression occurs in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Say: There have already come to you messengers before me with clear proofs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183].

[Page 416 continues]

"*Al-Bayyinat*" (the clear proofs) are the arguments indicating that what they call to is the will of Allah, and the miracles (*al-mu'jizat*) are included among the clear proofs.

The definiteness of "*al-Kitab*" (the Book) is the definiteness of genus (*ta'rif al-jins*), meaning: and We sent down with them books, i.e., like the Qur'an.

The sending down of the Book is the conveying of it through the angel from heaven, and the sending down of the Balance is the conveying of the command to justice among people.

"*Al-Mizan*" (the Balance) is used metaphorically for justice among people in giving them their rights, because what the balance requires is the existence of two sides whose equivalence is sought. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And when you judge between people, that you judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 58]. This Balance is what the books of the messengers explain, so its mention in particular is for the sake of emphasizing its importance, since it is the means by which the affairs of mankind are put in order, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you﴾ [al-Nisa': 105]. It is not meant that Allah inspired them to devise instruments of weighing, because this is not of primary importance, and it is among the things covered by the meaning of justice, so there is no need to draw attention to it specifically.

His saying ﴿that people may uphold justice﴾ is connected to "and We sent down with them."

"*Al-Qiyam*" (upholding, standing) is a metaphor for the goodness and straightness of conditions, because it is a cause of facilitating action, and this was previously discussed at His saying, Exalted: ﴿and who establish prayer﴾ at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

"*Al-Qist*" (justice) is justice in all affairs. It is more general than the mentioned Balance, because the Balance is specific to justice between two disputing parties, whereas "*al-qist*" is the conduct of people's affairs according to what truth requires. It is thus a general justice, such that the rightful owner is able to dispute with one who has taken possession of his right.

The word "*al-qist*" in Arabic is derived from the word *qistas*, which is the name for justice in the language of the Romans (Byzantines), so it is one of the Arabized words (*mu'arrab*). This is narrated from Mujahid.

The "*ba'*" (with) is for accompaniment (*mulabasah*), meaning: the affairs of people shall be accompanied by justice and conform to the truth. The sending down of iron is a metaphor for creating its ore, as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight kinds of livestock in pairs﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], meaning: He created them for your sake. This is through inspiring mankind to use it in weapons, such as swords, coats of mail, spears, arrows, helmets, shields, and maces.

[Page 417]

It is also possible that by "iron" is meant specifically the weapons made from it, such as swords, spear-heads and arrows, in which case the sending down of it is a metaphor for merely inspiring the making of it. According to the first interpretation, the pronoun in ﴿in which is great might﴾ refers to iron in view of its being prepared for might, so it is as though the might were contained within it.

"*Al-Ba's*" (might, force) is harm. What is meant is the force of killing and wounding by iron instruments such as swords, spears and arrows, and the force of people's boldness in inflicting harm on others by means of protective gear made of iron.

"*Al-Manafi'*" (benefits) are the benefits of the victor through iron, such as spoils of war, captives, and the conquest of lands.

The phrase "*lil-nas*" (for people) is connected to both "*ba's*" and "*manafi'*" by way of the construction of contention (*al-tanazu'*), meaning: in it is might for some people and benefits for others, since the calamities of one people are the gains of another.

The purpose of this is to draw the attention of the listeners to take heed of the wisdom of Allah, Exalted, in creating iron and inspiring its manufacture, and to alert them that its benefit and its might are intended to be placed where its might is deserved and its benefit is placed where it is fitting, not that its benefits be given to those who do not deserve them, such as highway robbers and rebels against the people of justice, nor for equipping armies to protect the homelands from those who transgress, nor for storing in homes to repel predators and aggressors against sanctities and property.

The Greek sage (Antisthenes), disciple of Socrates, when he saw a wealthy adorned woman in Athens, would go to her husband's house and ask him to show him his horse and his weapons. If he saw them both complete, he would permit his wife to adorn herself, because her husband was able to protect her from a corrupter who would abduct her; otherwise he would order her to abandon adornment and jewelry.

This is of the category of blocking the means (*sadd al-dhari'ah*), not so that its might is used to suppress the strength of justice and of those who enjoin what is right into silence, for that is a distortion of what Allah intended in placing beneficial and firm things. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205], and He said through the tongue of one of His messengers: ﴿I only intend reform as much as I am able﴾ [Hud: 88].

[Page 418]

This meaning has been alluded to in general by His saying: ﴿and so that Allah may make evident who supports Him and His messengers unseen﴾, meaning: so that He may show people the effect of Allah's knowledge of who supports Him. The verb "*li-ya'lama*" (so that He may know) is used in the sense of the manifestation of the effect of knowledge, like the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i:

*And I came while the spear swayed between us, so that I might know which of them is a coward and which a brave one.*

That is: so that the coward and the brave might become evident to people, meaning, so that they may know that I am their brave one.

The people's support of Allah is the support of His religion. As for Allah, He is free of need for support. The conjunction "*wa-rusulahu*" (and His messengers) is an addition, meaning: whoever supports those who uphold His religion. This includes supporting the laws of the Messenger ﷺ after him, and supporting the rulers of the affairs of the Muslims who uphold the truth. The greatest man who supported the religion of Allah after the death of His Messenger ﷺ was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, in his fighting the people of apostasy (*ahl al-riddah*).

His saying "*bil-ghayb*" (unseen) is connected to "*yansuruhu*" (supports Him): that is, he supports Him with a support which his own self drives him to, without fear of any inducer who urges him to it, or of an observer who watches his conduct. The meaning is that he strives in the way of Allah and in defending the religion with pure sincerity.

The mention of iron, its ore and its manufacture has already been made in the interpretation of His saying, Exalted: ﴿Bring me sheets of iron﴾ [al-Kahf: 96] in Surat al-Kahf.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Powerful, Mighty﴾ is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the clause ﴿We sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾ through to its end, meaning: because Allah is Powerful and Mighty in His holy affairs, so His messengers must likewise be strong and honored, and His books must be exalted and revered. This only comes about in this world, whose events are attached to the causes He has established, by His messengers and by sincere people to Allah supporting Him and assisting in spreading His religion and laws.

"*Al-Qawiyy al-'Aziz*" (the Powerful, the Mighty) are among His names, Exalted. "*Al-Qawiyy*" means one characterized by strength; He, Exalted, said: ﴿the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 58], and "*al-qawiyy*" was discussed previously in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is strong and severe in punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 52].

"*Al-'Aziz*" means one characterized by might ('izzah), which was discussed in His saying: ﴿Indeed, might belongs to Allah entirely﴾ [Yunus: 65] in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His saying: ﴿And know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 209].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 26:

Page 419

﴿And We had already sent Noah and Abraham, and placed in their offspring prophethood and the Scripture; so among them is one who is guided, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ This is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the clause ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], using the specific to conjoin the general (ʿataf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm), because a detailed explanation of its summary was intended, a detail through which the deviation of the polytheists among the Arabs and the astray among the Jews from the methods of their two forefathers, Noah and Abraham, is recorded. God, Most High, said concerning the Children of Israel: ﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah. Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra: 3]. The Arabs did not forget that they too are of the offspring of Noah, as al-Nabigha said praising al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir:

*So you found trustworthiness, and it had not betrayed you; likewise was Noah, who did not betray.*

Prophethood in their offspring is like the prophethood of Hud, Salih, Tubba', and the prophethood of Isma'il, Ishaq, Shu'ayb, and Ya'qub.

By "the Scripture" is meant what was in the hands of the offspring of Noah and the offspring of Abraham of the books containing the foundations of their religion, from the scrolls of Abraham and what they preserved of the injunctions of his and of Isma'il's and Ishaq's.

Fisq (defiant disobedience) means departing from guidance. Among the defiantly disobedient are the polytheists of 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot, Yemen, the Aws and the Khazraj, who are of the offspring of Noah, and of Midian, the Hijaz, and Tihama, who are of the offspring of Abraham.

What is meant is those who committed shirk before the coming of Islam, due to His saying: ﴿Then We followed up after them with Our messengers, and We followed up with Jesus, son of Mary﴾ [al-Hadid: 27].

[p. 420]

﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps, Our messengers; and We sent after them Jesus, son of Mary, and gave him the Gospel, and placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy. But monasticism, which they invented, We did not prescribe for them; they sought only the pleasure of God, yet they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

(Then) indicates gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because the mission of the messengers of God who came after Noah and Abraham and those of their descendants who preceded them was greater than what existed among the descendants of Abraham before the sending of the messengers whom God followed up, since they were sent to many nations, such as ʿAd, Thamud and the Children of Israel, and among them was a great law, which is the law of the Torah.

Taqfiyah (following up) means sending one messenger after another. It is derived from qafa (the back of the neck/back), because the one who comes after him comes as if walking from behind him. This was already discussed in His words, ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book and followed up after him with messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:87], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-athar (the traces, sing. athar) is the plural of athar, which is what a traveller leaves of the places his feet touched on the earth. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So they returned, retracing their footsteps﴾ [al-Kahf 18:64].

The plural pronoun in His words ʿala athariham ("upon their traces") refers to Noah, Abraham and their descendants, among whom were prophethood and the Book. Those among whom prophethood existed are many, and those among whom the Book existed are like the Children of Israel.

ʿAla ("upon") here indicates elevation. The original sense of qaffa ʿala atharihi ("he followed upon his trace") shows the closeness between the two walkers: the second walker arrives before the trace of the first has disappeared. This usage became common until qawluhum ʿala atharihi came to mean "shortly after him" or "his affair closely linked to the affair of his predecessor." This is an introduction for the community that God sent many messengers in general terms, and it prepares for the intended mention of the last messenger who came before Islam, namely Jesus, peace be upon him.

In repeating the verb qaffayna and not repeating ʿala athariham there is an indication of the long period between the last messengers of the Children of Israel and Jesus. The last messenger of the Children of Israel was Jonah son of Matthew, who was sent to the people of Nineveh at the beginning of the eighth century BCE. Therefore Jesus was not sent "upon the traces" of those who came before him.

Al-Injil (the Gospel) is the revelation that God sent down to Jesus and that his disciples (al-hawariyyun) wrote down in the course of relating his biography.

Al-Injil, with the hamza pronounced with kasra or fatha, is a loanword (muʿarrab), whose explanation was given earlier at the beginning of Surat Al ʿImran.

The meaning of placing compassion and mercy in the hearts of those who followed him is that the teachings of the Gospel which God gave to Jesus commanded them to adopt compassion and mercy, so they acted upon them; or that their training by the conduct of Jesus, peace be upon him, made these firmly rooted in their hearts, and this is by God's making it so, since He commanded them to it and made it easy for them.

That is because Jesus was sent to refine the souls of the Jews and to uproot the harshness from their hearts, which they had acquired over long generations. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they became like stones or even harder﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:74], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ra'fah (compassion) is mercy connected with averting harm and distress, so it is a special kind of mercy. It was discussed in His words, ﴿Indeed, God is Kind and Merciful to people﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143], in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His words, ﴿and let not compassion for them overtake you in the religion of God﴾ [al-Nur 24:2], in Surat al-Nur.

Al-rahmah (mercy) is tenderness and gentleness, and it was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Fatihah.

Thus the conjunction of mercy after compassion is the conjunction of the general after the specific, to encompass its kinds after having given attention to some of them.

Al-rahbaniyyah (monasticism) is a noun for the state in which the monk (al-rahib) is characterised in most matters of his religion. It contains the nisba ya' (relative suffix) attached to al-rahib contrary to the regular analogy, since the regular nisba to al-rahib would be al-rahibiyyah. The nun in it is added for emphasis in the nisba, just as it was added in their saying shaʿrani (very hairy), for one who has much hair; liḥyani (of a great beard); ruhani (spiritual); and nasrani (Christian).

Al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) made the nun come from the description rahban, like the nun of khashyan from khashiya, and the emphasis is the same, except that it is emphasis in the description and not in the intensity of the nisba.

The ta' (ha') in it is the feminine ending, with the word treated as a noun denoting the state. Al-Kashshaf made the ha' indicate the single occurrence (al-marrah).

As for the name of the monk to whom al-rahbaniyyah is attributed, it is a descriptive adjective treated as a proper noun: he is the worshipper among the Christians who devotes himself wholly to worship. It is a derivative of al-rahab, meaning fear, because he is greatly fearful of the anger of God, the Exalted, or of violating the Christian religion. In the customary usage of the Christians, this state entails withdrawal from people, avoiding whatever distracts from worship, and that is achieved by dwelling in hermitages and monasteries and abstaining from marriage to avoid distractions. Some groups of monks may have made abstention from marriage obligatory upon the monk out of extremism in religion.

Al-Kashshaf also said: al-rahbaniyyah is derived from al-rahab, meaning fear of tyrants, that is, those Jews who did not believe in Jesus, peace be upon him. The tyrants overcame the believers in Jesus and fought them three times until only a few of them remained. So they feared that they would be tempted in their religion, and they chose monasticism, which is their withdrawal into the mountains, fleeing from the temptation in religion. End of quotation.

The first persecution of the followers of the Messiah appeared in the land of Judea. When the followers of the Messiah and their followers scattered in the regions, the people of polytheism and idolatry among the Romans attacked them wherever they settled in the lands under their rule. Thus conditions of taqiyyah (concealment of faith under compulsion) arose among them, which is what the author of al-Kashshaf called "fighting the tyrants."

So the monk abstains from marriage for fear that his wife would distract him from his worship; he avoids mixing with companions for fear that they would divert him from worship; and he forgoes the pleasures of food and clothing for fear that he would fall into acquiring unlawful wealth. They wanted to imitate Jesus, peace be upon him, in asceticism regarding this world and in abstaining from marriage. Therefore God, the Exalted, said "they invented them" (ibtada'uha), that is, they originated them, for ibtida' is bringing in a bid'ah (innovation), and bida' are things that were not known before. That is, they originated them after their messenger. For bid'ah is that which is newly introduced after the lawgiver.

Al-rahbaniyyah is in the accusative by the construction of ishtighal (the verb being implied with a pronoun referring to the object). The estimated sense is: "and they invented monasticism."

[p. 423]

It is not coordinated with compassion and mercy, because this monasticism was not something God prescribed for them, so it cannot be the object of "We placed" (jaʿalna). Also, monasticism is an action that is not connected to the hearts, whereas the verb "We placed" is restricted by ﴿in the hearts of those who followed him﴾, so its objects would be restricted accordingly, unless one interprets placing it in the hearts as placing love for it, as in His words, ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:93].

On this grammatical analysis (iʿrab) the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) went, such as Abu ʿAli al-Farisi, al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that it could be coordinated with "compassion and mercy." Ibn ʿAtiyyah accused this analysis of being the analysis of the Mu'tazilah, saying: "The Mu'tazilah analyse 'monasticism' as accusative by an implied verb that is explained by 'they invented them,' and they go in that direction because they hold that a person creates his own actions, so they analyse the verse accordingly." End of quotation. There is no proof for them in this analysis, nor is there any benefit in refuting it, since they differ from it, as you know.

This sentence was coordinated with the sentence ﴿and We placed in the hearts of those who followed him﴾ only because the two sentences share the feature that it is among the virtues whose purpose is the pleasure of God.

The meaning: they invented for themselves monasticism, which We did not prescribe for them, but they sought by it the pleasure of God, so God accepted it from them, because the context of the narration about them requires praise of them in their conditions.

The pronoun of the subject in "they invented them" refers to those who followed Jesus. The meaning: they originated the practice of it, so it does not follow that all of them invented the method of monasticism; rather, some of them may have established it and the rest followed him.

"Those who followed him" applies to all who adhered to Christianity, but the highest of their ranks are those who were guided by his conduct with complete guidance and devoted themselves to it, and they are those who perform worship.

The bringing of the relative pronoun with its relative clause indicates that the placing of compassion and mercy in their hearts is a consequence of their following his way and their devotion to him.

The sentence "We did not prescribe it for them" explains the sentence "they invented them." His words "except seeking the pleasure of God" are a safeguard (ihtiras) against misunderstanding, and the three sentences together form a digression and an interjection (istitrad wa iʿtiraḍ).

The exception with His words ﴿except seeking the pleasure of God﴾ is interposed between the sentence ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ and the sentence "so they did not observe it."

This is a disjunctive exception (istithna munqati'), and the disjunctive exception is included in the governing rule of the operator upon the excepted noun, even if the wording of the excepted noun does not include it. The meaning of its being disjunctive is that it is disconnected from the meaning of the preceding noun, not from its governing operator. So the exception requires that "seeking the pleasure of God" be semantically an object of the verb "We prescribed it," so the meaning is: "but We prescribed for them the seeking of God's pleasure," that is, that they should seek God's pleasure through every deed, not specifically the monasticism which they invented. That is, God did not impose on them that very thing.

His words ﴿except seeking the pleasure of God﴾ may be a negation of God's imposition of it, even within the general scope of what includes it, that is, it is not among what is covered by the command to seek God's pleasure, and they assumed that they pleased God by it. It may also be a negation of some aspects of the prescription being written upon them, namely the writing of a command to it specifically, so monasticism would be among what is sought for the pleasure of God, that is, they prescribed it upon themselves to realise what contains God's pleasure. This is like His words, ﴿except what Israel forbade himself before the Torah was sent down﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:93], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Be strict, and God will be strict upon them," in the story of slaughtering the cow. This is the apparent meaning of the verse.

"Seeking" (ibtighaʾ) is in the accusative as the object of the verb "We prescribed," and you may make it an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) by an implied verb after the exception particle, that is: "but they invented it for the sake of seeking God's pleasure."

In the verse, according to the more apparent of the two possibilities, there is an indication of the legitimacy of tahqiq al-manat (verification of the applicability of a cause to particular instances), which is establishing the effective cause (ʿillah) in its individual particulars and establishing the legal principle in its applications.

In it there is evidence for the division of innovation (bid'ah) into praiseworthy and blameworthy, according to its being subsumed under some kind of legal provision, so the five legal categories apply to it, as al-Shihab al-Qarafi and the skilled scholars verified. As for those who tried to restrict it to blame, they found no outlet. ʿUmar said, when the people were gathered behind one reciter during the night prayers of Ramadan: "What a good innovation this is."

It has been said that they invented monasticism to separate from the communities of polytheism among the Greeks and Romans and from the oppression of the Jews. It is evident that this is a seeking of God's pleasure, as God related about the People of the Cave: ﴿And when you have withdrawn from them and what they worship other than God, retreat to the cave﴾ [al-Kahf 18:16]. In a hadith: "It will soon be that the best property of a Muslim will be sheep with which he follows the mountain tops and the places where rain falls, fleeing with his religion from trials." On this basis, marriage would be an accidental matter required by withdrawal from cities and communities, but those who came after them assumed it to be a fundamental principle of monasticism.

As for Jesus's abstention from marriage, it was perhaps due to another circumstance for which God commanded him, and abstention from marriage is not among the affairs of prophethood, for all the prophets had wives. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We gave them wives and offspring﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:38].

It was also said: their innovation of monasticism (al-rahbaniyya) consisted in their vowing it to God. Abstaining from worldly pleasures and inflicting hardship upon the self were among the means of drawing near to God in some of the earlier revealed laws, and they remained in place until Islam abolished them, as in the hadith on vows in the Muwatta': "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw a man standing in the sun, silent, and he asked about him. They said: He vowed not to speak, not to seek shade, and to fast his day. He said: Tell him to speak, to seek shade, and to complete his fast, for God is not in need of this man's tormenting himself." Already in the surah of Maryam God's words have passed: ﴿So say: I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak to any human today﴾ [Maryam: 26]. There is no contradiction between the two statements, because the causes of monasticism have multiplied according to the differences of religions.

Following from His words "they innovated it" and ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾, and what comes after it, is His words ﴿but they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾. That is: as a consequence of their undertaking monasticism, those who committed themselves to monasticism did not observe it with its due observance. The apparent meaning of the verse is that all of them fell short, to varying degrees, in discharging its right. It also implies that what God prescribes for His servants of obligations does not impose hardship on people in acting upon it.

Al-ri'ayah (observance) means preservation, that is: they did not preserve it with the proper preservation. Preservation is used figuratively for fulfilling what the nature of the act requires. Monasticism revolves around turning away from fleeting pleasures and training oneself to endure abstention from beloved things, lest diversion by them preoccupy one from worship and from reflection on the signs of

God. So when there is shortfall in committing to it at some times, or neglect in some of its forms, the right of its preservation is lost.

"Haqqa ri'ayatihā" (its due observance) is an idafa of an attribute to its qualified noun, meaning: its observance of the right.

The right (haqq) of a thing is its occurrence in the most perfect condition of its kind, and it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) specifying the kind.

The meaning is: they did not preserve the affairs of monasticism with complete preservation. Thus the focus of the negation is the qualifier "its due observance."

This negation has many degrees, and the statement is directed as a reproach for their shortcoming in what they committed to or vowed, and that is a regression from the levels of perfection, whereas it is fitting for the God-fearing to be increasing in perfection.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most beloved religion to God is the most constant of it."

His words ﴿So We gave those among them who believed their reward﴾ are a consequence of the clause ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him﴾ up to the end, and what lies between them is a digression.

By "those who believed" is meant those characterized by faith as the Qur'an defines it, namely the affirmation of God's oneness and belief in His messengers in every age. That is: We gave those among those who followed him who believed their reward, namely those who did not mix their following of him with what corrupts it, like those who believed in the divinity of Jesus (peace be upon him) or his being the son of God, and those like them among the Christians who introduced into the religion what contradicts its foundations, and they are many among the Christians, as He said: ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Hadid: 16].

By "defiant disobedience" (fisq) is meant disbelief. This is a commendation of the sincere believers among those who passed away from the Christians before the Muhammadan mission and the arrival of its call to the Christians. Their claim to be followers of the Messiah is false, because they followed him only in outward form. Those who corrupted their faith by undermining its foundations are the intended referent of His words ﴿And many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Hadid: 16], that is: and many of those who undertook his religion have departed from faith. So the intended meaning of "fisq" encompasses disbelief and what falls short of it, like those who altered the Book and treated its laws lightly, as God said: ﴿O you who believe, indeed many of the rabbis and monks devour people's wealth by falsehood and bar from the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 57, verse 28:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy, and will appoint for you a light by which you will walk, and will forgive you. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

It is prevalent in the Qur'an that "those who have believed" (alladhina amanu) is a title for the believers in Muhammad ﷺ. However, since ﴿O you who have believed﴾ occurs here immediately after His saying ﴿So We gave those who believed among them their reward﴾ [al-Hadid: 27], i.e., among those who followed 'Isa (peace be upon him), the phrase ﴿O you who have believed﴾ may be understood in its title-like usage, namely as being, by dominance, like a proper name for the believers of the religion of Islam. It may also be understood in its broader linguistic usage, namely those from whom faith has come about, which here means those who believed in 'Isa. The more apparent view is that both of these possibilities are intended, so that the sincere Christians (khullas al-Nasara) may take their share from this speech, which is the call to them to believe in Muhammad ﷺ, so that they complete what preceded from their following of 'Isa. Thus the address is directed to those existing among those who believed in 'Isa, i.e.: O you who have believed with sincere faith in the law of 'Isa, fear Allah, dread His punishment, abandon partisanship (al-'asabiyya), envy and ill opinion, and believe in Muhammad ﷺ.

As for the possibility that ﴿those who have believed﴾ is meant in the general title-like sense, the believers of the Islamic religion take from it a glad tiding that their reward will not be less than the reward of the believers among the People of the Book, because when they believed in the earlier Messengers, Allah gave them the reward of the believers of their communities. His saying "and believe" (wa-aminu) is then used in the sense of persistence in faith, like His saying ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 136] in Surat al-Nisa'. In this possibility, the insertion of the command to taqwa is intentional, so that the speech contains a command to something that is renewed, followed by a command from which it is understood that the purpose is the seeking of persistence. This is among the wonders of the Qur'anic composition.

The meaning of Allah giving the believers from the community of Islam "a double portion (kiflayn)" of the reward is that they have the like of the reward of the two who believed from the People of the Book. The hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari from the Prophet ﷺ in Sahih al-Bukhari explains this, in which it says: "The likeness of the Muslims, the Jews and the Christians is like the likeness of a man who hired workers to work for him. The Jews worked until midday for a qirat, the Christians worked from midday until the afternoon prayer for a qirat, and then the Muslims worked from the afternoon prayer until sunset for two qirats." He said in it: "And they completed the reward of both groups." That is, they completed the like of the reward of both groups, i.e., they received double the reward of each group.

Taqwa of Allah relates to deeds and to belief, and to knowledge of the Shari'a. Our companions (the Shafi'is/jurists of our school) have derived the obligation of ijtihad for the one qualified for it from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16].

His saying "fear Allah" is a command to them with that which is a means and a preliminary to the intended matter, which is the command in His saying ﴿and believe in His Messenger﴾.

He then arranged upon this command what is the answer of an elided conditional clause, namely the sentence ﴿He will give you a double portion﴾ etc., the jussive in response to the command; i.e., He will give you a reward in the Hereafter and a reward in this world. The reward of the Hereafter is His saying ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ and His saying "and will forgive you", and the reward of this world is His saying ﴿and will appoint for you a light by which you will walk﴾.

Kifl (with a kasra on the kaf and a sukun on the fa') means a share. Its original sense is a doubled reward, and it is an arabicized word from Ethiopic, as Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said; i.e., He will give you two great rewards, and each of the two is double the other and equal to it, and therefore it is dualized as kiflayn, just as one says "zawj" for one of two that are similar. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment﴾ [al-Ahzab: 68] and His saying ﴿Her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. In the authentic hadith the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me, followed me and affirmed me, for him are two rewards," the hadith.

"From His mercy" is connected to "He will give you," and (min) is initial (ibtida'iyya) in a metaphorical sense, i.e., that is from Allah's mercy toward you. For the Christians this means, for their faith in Muhammad and their faith in 'Isa; i.e., it is from Allah's grace and generosity, since belief in Muhammad ﷺ is obligatory upon them just as their belief in 'Isa is, and it completes belief in 'Isa. Their reward is doubled because of the attachment of souls to what they adhere to, so that it is difficult for them to abandon it. As for the side of the Muslims, it is an honour for them, lest some of the Christians who believed in Muhammad ﷺ surpass them.

It is also permissible that "from His mercy" be an attribute of "kiflayn," and then (min) is explicative (bayaniyya), and the speech is according to an elision of a modifier, its estimate being: and it is the reward of Paradise and its bliss.

His saying ﴿and will appoint for you a light by which you will walk﴾ is a parable for the state of the people who seek attainment of Allah's good pleasure and success in bliss, and who fear falling into the opposite of that, by the state of a people walking on a road at night, fearing error in it, who are given a light by which they see the mountain passes and are safe from going astray. The meaning is: He will appoint for you a state like a state of light by which you walk, and the ba' is for instrumentality, like "I wrote with the pen."

The meaning is: He will facilitate for you a guidance by which you are guided to the truth.

All parts of this parable are suitable to be independent metaphors, and this is the most eloquent of the states of parable. The Qur'an has established the comparison of guidance with light, error with darkness, proof with a path, and the exercise of reflection with walking, and this became widespread after the Qur'an in the speech of Arabic literati.

Forgiveness is a reward for their compliance with what they were commanded, i.e., He will forgive you what has passed from you of disbelief and error.

Ahl al-Kitab (the People of the Book) is a title in the Qur'an for the Jews and Christians who did not adopt Islam, because "the Book" (al-Kitab), when it is joined to "ahl," refers to the Torah and the Gospel. So the term is not applied to Muslims as "ahl al-Kitab," even if they have a scripture. Whoever among the Jews and Christians becomes a Muslim is not described as "of the People of the Book" in the Qur'anic usage. For this reason, when 'Abdullah ibn Salam was described in the Qur'an, he was described with the words ﴿and whoever has with him knowledge of the Book﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 43], and with the words ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 10]. Since those who were spoken of earlier became believers in Muhammad (ﷺ), the description "People of the Book" departed from them, and it remained specific to the Jews and Christians. When God called those who followed the Messiah to faith in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), and promised them a doubling of the reward for that faith, He informed them that their faith nullifies what the followers of Christianity claim after that, of virtue and nobility for themselves, by their continuing to follow 'Isa (peace be upon him), so that they would deceive people into thinking that if the virtue of Islam escaped them, nothing of virtue was lost to them by following 'Isa, given that they had not changed their religion.

This meaning is conveyed by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That the People of the Book may know that they have no power over anything of the bounty of God﴾.

Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) said: Al-Wahidi said: "This is a difficult verse, and the exegetes have no clear statement about its connection to what precedes it," end quote. Is it connected to His saying ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [Al-Hadid: 28] and so on, or is it connected to ﴿So We gave those who believed among them their reward﴾ [Al-Hadid: 27] up to His saying ﴿And God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Al-Hadid: 28]? Al-Wahidi means that the connection of the verse to what precedes it determines the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That the People of the Book may know that they have no power over anything of the bounty of God﴾.

The lam in His saying ﴿That the People of the Book may know﴾ may be causative (lam al-ta'lil), so that what follows it is caused by what precedes it. On this reading, the particle (la) may be a superfluous particle added for emphasis and strengthening.

The thing being explained must necessarily be something that returns to the bounty of God, and that is what His saying contains: ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy and will make for you a light by which you will walk and forgive you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 28], or His saying ﴿So We gave those who believed among them their reward﴾ [Al-Hadid: 27] up to "Forgiving and Merciful."

The majority of exegetes went to treating (la) as superfluous, and that the meaning is affirmative, i.e., "so that he may know." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who read "liya'lama" (so that he may know), and also read "li-kay ya'lama" (in order that he may know), and his reading is an explanation. This is the view of al-Farra' and al-Akhfash, and az-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf, Ibn 'Atiyya, and Ibn Hisham in Mughni al-Labib followed it. This rests on the premise that (la) may occur superfluously, which al-Akhfash affirmed, and of which there are His sayings: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92], and His saying ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 12], and His saying ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [Al-Waqi'a: 75], and similar. And His saying: ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We destroyed that they will not return﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 95], according to one of the interpretations. It is also related that the Arabs used it as filler in the verse of the poet recited by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala':

"His generosity refused, not stinginess, and "yes" was hastened by him from a youth whose speaker does not withhold generosity."

In one transmission, "al-bukhl" (stinginess) is in the accusative. The Arabs interpreted the line to mean: "His generosity refused stinginess."

The meaning on this view is that the cause is the conveying of this news to the People of the Book, so that they may know that the bounty of God was given to others, so that they do not boast that they possess a virtue that is not less than the virtue of others, since others have a virtue. This is consistent with the interpretation of Mujahid and Qatada.

In my view, this does not yield a meaning, because the Qur'an's report that the Muslims have a double reward is not believed by the People of the Book, so their knowledge does not settle on the idea that they have no virtue. How then can God's report about it be explained as removing the knowledge of the People of the Book of the virtue of themselves, so that they know that they have no virtue?

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani went, and a group followed him, to the view that (la) is a negation particle. Al-Fakhr established this by saying that the pronoun in "yaqdirun" (they have power) refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and those who believed in him (i.e., by way of iltifat, the shift from address to third person, and its original form was "an la taqdiru" [that you have no power]). When the knowledge of the People of the Book that the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Muslims have no power over anything of the bounty of God is negated, the opposite of that is established in their knowledge, i.e., how the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Muslims have power over the bounty of God. "Yaqdirun" (they have power) is then metaphorically used with the meaning "they attain," and "the bounty is in the hand of God," so He is the One who gave them virtue, and this is a kinaya (metonymy) for the negation of virtue from the People of the Book who did not believe in the Messenger (ﷺ).

This interpretation is subject to the same objection as the previous one, because the knowledge of the People of the Book is not obtained by the Qur'an's report, since they deny it.

I see that the claim that (la) is superfluous has no need for it, and that keeping it to its original meaning, which is negation, is required. The lam is taken as lam al-'aqiba (the lam of consequence), i.e., "We gave you this virtue and it was withheld from the People of the Book, so the People of the Book remained in their ignorance and delusion that they have a lasting virtue, and they do not come to know that they do not possess God's bounty, nor that God has given the virtue to another people and withheld it from them, so they forget that the bounty is in the hand of God, and no one deserves it by essence."

With this delusion they continued to hold fast to their ancient religion. It is known that the lam of consequence originally is a figurative causation, as you know from its treatment in the exegesis of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up to become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8] in Surat al-Qasas.

His saying "ahl al-Kitab" may refer to the Jews alone if the causation is taken as causation for the whole of His saying ﴿So We gave those who believed among them their reward﴾ [Al-Hadid: 27] and His saying ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [Al-Hadid: 28]. It may also refer to the Jews and Christians if the lam of causation is taken as the cause for His saying ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾ [Al-Hadid: 28].

The (an) in His saying "an la yaqdirun" (that they have no power) is the lightened form of (anna), and its subject is a omitted pronoun of matter (damir al-sha'n).

The meaning is: Do not be concerned with the People of the Book's lack of knowledge that they have no power over anything of the bounty of God, and that the bounty is in the hand of God, He gives it to whom He wills. That is: do not be concerned with their compound ignorance in persisting in their deception that they have a standing with God, Exalted is He, for God knows this, and it is their disposition, so they do not desist from it. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God has sealed upon their hearts﴾ [Al-Baqara: 7] in Surat al-Baqara.

The sentence ﴿And God is Possessor of great bounty﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) encompassing the bounty that God gave to the People of the Book who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and other bounty.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Surat al-Mujadila. This surah is named in the books of exegesis, in the mushafs, and in the books of Sunna "Surat al-Mujadila" with a kasra or a fatha on the dal, as will come. It is also called "Surat Qad Sami'a" (the surah of "Indeed He has heard"), and this name is well known in the kuttab (Qur'an schools) in Tunisia, and in the mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it was called "Surat al-Zihar" (the surah of zihar).

The reason it is called "Surat al-Mujadila" is that it opens with the matter of the dispute of the wife of Aws ibn al-Samit before the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the zihar (the pronouncement of her husband).

The exegetes and commentators of the books of Sunna did not mention its vocalization, whether with a kasra or a fatha on the dal. Al-Khafaji, in his gloss on al-Baydawi, reported from al-Kashf that the kasra of the dal is the known form (but I do not know what al-Khafaji meant by the Kashf to which he attributed this). The Kashf of al-Qazwini on al-Kashshaf does not contain this, nor does the exegesis called al-Kashf wa al-Bayan of al-Tha'labi. Perhaps al-Khafaji saw it in the Kashf from which al-Tibi quotes in places of restatements of the words of al-Kashshaf, and it is not known among the commentaries on al-Kashshaf. The kasra of the dal is more apparent, because the surah opens with mention of she who disputes about her husband, so it is more fitting that it be attributed to the one who disputes, who is the one God mentioned by His saying ﴿She who disputes with you concerning her husband﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 1]. I saw in a copy of the gloss of Muhammad al-Hamadhani on al-Kashshaf, called Tawdih al-Mushkilat, in the handwriting of its author, that he placed a kasra mark beneath the dal of "al-Mujadila." As for the fatha of the dal, it is a verbal noun (masdar) taken from the verb ﴿disputes with you﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 1], as He expressed it with "tahawur" (dialogue) in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God hears your dialogue﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 1].

This surah is Medinan, said Ibn 'Atiyya, by consensus. In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, from 'Ata': the first ten verses of it are Medinan and the rest are Meccan. In it, from al-Kalbi: it is Medinan except His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is their fourth﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 7] up to the end of the verse, which was revealed in Mecca.

[Page 6]

It is the one hundred and third surah in the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Munafiqun and before Surat al-Tahrim.

What appears is that Surat al-Mujadila was revealed before Surat al-Ahzab, because God, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿And He has not made your wives whom you declare unlawful as your mothers﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 4]. That requires that this verse was revealed after the annulment of the ruling of zihar by what is in Surat al-Mujadila, because His saying "ma ja'ala" (He has not made) requires the annulment of prohibition by zihar. It was annulled only by the verse of Surat al-Mujadila. As-Sakhawi said: Surat al-Mujadila was revealed after Surat al-Munafiqun and before Surat al-Hujurat.

Its verses number twenty-one according to the count of the people of Medina and Mecca, and twenty-two according to the count of the people of Syria, Basra and Kufa.
